speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: Owing to certain changes having been made by parliamentary counsel in the drafting of this bill which, while not changing the meaning of the measure, make it different and more difficult to explain, I move that the bill be discharged from the order paper with a view to possible redrafting and resubmission to the House.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Will the minister explain how the bill is more difficult to explain if the meaning is not changed?

As drafted by parliamentary counsel portions of the former bill were inserted that were not in the bill submitted to me. That makes the bill appear quite different from what was contemplated, and the intention of the draftsman and counsel would be more difficult to explain.

Perhaps the minister would not object to informing the House in what respect the bill has been changed? I understand it has been arranged for a motion to be moved this afternoon which will prevent this bill from going into effect this session. It depends on the result of the debate which takes place and the motion of my hon. friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll); and the minister ought to explain to the House whether he is a consenting party to having this part of the bill obliterated, and be dependent upon the result of the motion which is to be debated this afternoon.

In compliance with the hon. member's request, I have in my hand the bill as redrafted, and an initialled
copy got out by parliamentary counsel. The original draft reads as follows:
2. Section five of the said act is amended by adding at the end of paragraph Ob) thereof the words "or less than eighty per centum of milk fat"; and by striking out, in paragraph (c) thereof, in the second line the words "what is generally known as", and in the third line thereof the words "nor add any milk or cream or butter".
The draft incorporated by parliamentary counsel and not to be found in the original act as submitted to my department and by myself to this House reads:
5. No person shall-
(a)	manufacture, import into Canada, or offer, sell or have in his possession for sale, any oleomargarine, margarine, butterine, or other substitute for butter, manufactured wholly or in part from any fat other than that of milk or cream;

The parliamentary counsel takes the position that that makes the section more intelligible.	I take	the	ground Mr.	Speaker,

Section 3, Notwithstanding anything contained in The Dairy	Industry	Act,	1914, chapter	7 of the
statutes of 1914, or in any other statute or law, the manufacture in and importation of oleomargarine into Canada-

With regard to the

Mr. SPEAKER I must remind the House that the motion is not debatable because it can only be made by unanimous consent. As there is no unanimous consent, no debate can take place. Let me call the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to page 541 of Bourinot, where he says:
XX. Bills once introduced, not altered except by authority of the House.
While a bill is in progress in the Commons no alteration whatever can be made in its provisions, except by the authority of the House. If it should be found that the bill has been materially altered since its introduction it would have to be withdrawn. A clerical alteration, however, is admissible. If it be necessary to make any changes in the bill before the second reading, the member in charge of it will ask *!eave to withdraw the bill and present another instead thereof.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I beg to move that the
House do now proceed to notice of motion No. 9, in the name of the member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll), respecting oleomargarine.

I rise to a point of order and would calle the attention of the House to Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules, section 423, which says:
A motion must not anticipate a matter already appointed for consideration by the House, such as the subject matter of a bill on the order paper.
The motion now before the House is one dealing with the subject matter of a bill which stands in the name of the hon. Minister of Agriculture. Consequently, I contend, it would be out of order to proceed with this resolution.

I should like to hear the opinion of some of the older members on the point of order, but I feel inclined to declare the point well taken. If the bill introduced by the hon. Minister of Agriculture had been withdrawn, then under rule No. 36, the motion of the member for Cape Breton South could have been debated, but as the bill is still before the House and deals directly with the subject matter of the resolution in the name of the hon. member for Cape Breton South, I think that the point is well taken. Beauchesne's Section 423 under Rule No. 42 says:
A motion must not anticipate a matter already appointed for consideration by the House, such as the subject matter of a bill on the order paper.
The bill introduced by the Minister of Agriculture-

On what date was
the bill introduced?

The bill was introduced
on the 28th May and is still before the House No action has yet been taken and I conceive the objection arising in the mind of the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland). This motion was put on the order paper before this bill, but no action was taken on it. It is still there. It could have been withdrawn any day by the hon. member. On the other hand the bill which deals with the same question, in one of its sections, was duly introduced in the House on the 28th May. Action was therefore taken on this bill, first by its being introduced, then by its first reading, and finally the second reading was fixed for to-day. Therefore it stands for consideration before the House. I find in that bill clause 2, which reads:
Section 5 of the said act is repealed, and the following is substituted therefor:
"5. No person shall-(a) manufacture, import into Canada, or offer, sell or have in his possession for sale, any oleomargarine, margarine, butterine, or other substitute for butter, manufactured wholly or in part from any fat other than that of milk or cream."
That is exactly the subject matter of the motion standing in the name of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll), and as that bill is not yet withdrawn and is, according to the rules, before the House, the motion cannot be debated to-day because it would be, according to the authority above quoted, "anticipating a matter already appointed for consideration by this House."
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals): Mr. Speaker, might I be permitted to say a word before you give

Oleomargarine
your ruling? I imagine the rules of the House are intended to be practical. If the rule was violated by any person, it was not by the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll), but by the minister. If the ruling be correct that the introduction of a bill, after notice of a resolution, will prevent the discussion of that resolution, then any resolution introduced in this House can be stopped by some person introducing a bill. It seems to me that the priority in this case should apply to the resolution. I can understand the rule to mean that the bill could not be proceeded with so long as the resolution stood in the way, but I cannot understand the practicability of a rule which would permit any member of parliament to stop a resolution being discussed by merely introducing a bill.

And then withdrawing
it.
Yes, he could withdraw it.

I am pleased indeed to express my opinion, not meaning at all that it is thorough or mature. So far as I understand the resolution, I quite support the inclination of the Chair. The rule has been read, and it provides specifically that no motion may be made that affects the subject matter of a bill appointed for consideration. This bill has been dealt with by the House. Not only has leave to introduce been moved and passed; but a first reading has been moved and passed, and the bill has been appointed by the House for second reading. Consequently no motion, certainly no motion not heretofore dealt with, can be taken up that deals with the subject matter of the bill. The hon. member says that if anyone has broken the rule, it is the minister. Nobody has broken the rule.
I mean the spirit of it.

Nor the spirit of it. The minister has introduced the bill; he has had it dealt with; he has had it dealt with at a first reading. There is nothing in the rule which prevents that being done. Supposing what my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) says is right, any hon. member by the mere fact of putting a motion on the order paper can stop legislation; he can stop effective legislation. A motion gets us nowhere save to the conclusion of agreement or disagreement ; it does not bring about legislation. An hon. member by placing a motion on the order paper and by holding it there until the end of the session, could prevent the House
from moving by way of legislation. The rule takes care that that cannot be done, and consequently I think the point is well taken and should be upheld.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not rise to discuss the ruling at all. I concur in it. I submit this, that the question of oleomargarine must be discussed. Therefore, why cannot we waive the rule so as to let us discuss it and thus settle the matter?

-and perhaps this

speakeroldname: Mr. W. F. CARROLL (Cape Breton South and Richmond):
speechtext:
I do not pretend for a moment to know the rules of the House as re-
Oleomargarine

gards procedure; but it strikes me as a sort of commonsense man, that the objection of the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) is not just what I would expect from a man of my own calibre, that is, a man of common sense. May I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is a measure that must be preceded by a resolution? I do not pretend to be in the same class as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), who will one day introduce a bill and then ask leave of the House to withdraw it-I am not saying that in any carping or criticizing way. But supposing that method were carried on in this House, does the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) think it would get us anywhere?
We did not let him withdraw it.

No, that is the trouble. My right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) has been criticizing more or less the action of the government in refusing to bring in the question of oleomargarine, and I would say, correctly so, if I were allowed to say that. He has the opportunity to-day, by consenting, by making the consent of the House unanimous, to allowing the Minister of Agriculture to withdraw his bill, of allowing us to go on if Mr. Speaker's ruling is right, and discussing the question of oleomargarine.
Coming back again to the question of the resolution, I think on two or three occasions questions of this kind have come before the House. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), I think it was, on April 14, 1920, made a motion in this House regarding the Water Carriage of Goods Act, and he was told by the Speaker at that time that that motion would have to be preceded by a resolution. At that time there was on the order paper a bill dealing with that very motion much more advanced than is the bill of the Minister of Agriculture.
Then again, a gentleman who is now in the Senate, Mr. McCoig, on May 6, 1920, was balked in proceeding with a bill regarding the standardization of agricultural machinery. There was on the order paper at that time legislation in the form of a tariff resolution.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, what would be the result if your ruling in this particular instance were right?-I hasten to assure you, Sir, that I am not criticizing your ruling; but you desire the opinions of hon. members and I am simply giving my own humble view of the situation. My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) has asked, I presume, with perfect sincerity, that he be allowed to with-
draw his bill, and the House has refused to give its unanimous consent to that withdrawal. Now, Sir, I contend, notwithstanding the quotation you have submitted1, that any hon. member may withdraw any bill standing in his name, and is not bound to proceed with it. The Minister of Agriculture says: I desire to withdraw my bill; I am going to bring in another one at some future time and therefore I shall not proceed with the one at present on the order paper. Who is the arbiter on that question? Is it the House, or is it the hon. gentleman who, having introduced the bill, finds that circumstances are such as to suggest the advisability of his withdrawing it? If he does not wish to proceed with his bill, and the House is not willing to give its unanimous consent to its withdrawal, is it contended that any hon. member is precluded from taking up a resolution which was on the order paper in his name long before the date at which the minister's bill appeared thereon? I ask, is it fair or just that an hon. member should be deprived of the opportunity of discussing a resolution, under such circumstances as I have just stated, simply because the Minister of Agriculture saw fit to introduce at a later date, a bill touching largely the same subject?
I would ask the hon. member this: How many times has this resolution been called since it was first placed on the order paper?

It has never been called
except on a single occasion, and at that, it was called at five minutes to six on a Wednesday afternoon, when I naturally refused to proceed with the consideration of it. As a matter of fact, I think that certain hon. members in this House so calculated their time as to have my resolution called at that particular moment. As I say, I naturally refused to go on with a subject of the importance which I attach to this question; certainly I could not have done justice to it in five minutes, and no one could have expected to attempt to take it up on that occasion. I daresay that had it been discussed at all, the good judgment of the House would have favoured the manufacture of oleomargarine. The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) has said that the minister's bill was appointed for second reading. Well, the minister's judgment was that the second reading should not be gone on with. He said, in so many words: I do not wish to go ahead with my bill; I propose to withdraw it. Under all the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, and with all due deference to what I consider the tenour of your ruling, I submit that it is absolutely unjust that an hon. member should be pro-

Oleomargarine
hibited-even though prohibition may be advisable in some respects-from exercising what I believe to be his right in this particular instance.

I think, Mr. Speaker, that we have had too much quibbling over technicalities in this House, involving too great a waste of time. While I bow to your ruling, I feel with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) that the House should give its unanimous consent and concede to the hon. member the right to proceed.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Pictou, Acting Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
It seems to
me, Mr. Speaker, that under the rules the hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Carroll) would be quite in order in going on with his motion. Your Honour has cited the following rule:
A motion must not anticipate a matter already appointed for consideration by the House, such as the subject matter of a bill on the order paper.
What is the situation here? My hon. friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll) placed on the order paper at a certain stage in the session a certain resolution which, at that time, conflicted with no other motion before the House. The resolution when the hon. member placed it on the order paper did not anticipate any bill that had already been appointed for consideration by the House, and the hon. member therefore had the undoubted right at any time when opportunity offered to move the resolution. There is no authority that I can find either in Bourinot or in Beauchesne by which it can be contended that the later introduction of a bill can deprive an hon. member of the right to proceed with a motion which has precedence of it.
Priority obtains.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
The whole
thing turns upon the point as to when the minister's bill was appointed for the consideration of the House. It was not appointed for such consideration prior to the time that my hon. friend's motion appeared on the order paper; therefore, that hon. gentleman had the prior right to proceed with his resolution. I submit, therefore, that hon. gentlemen, viewing the matter in the light of these circumstances, should give their unanimous consent that the hon. gentleman be allowed to discuss his motion.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I wish to add a word,
Mr. Speaker, on another point, I would observe, in answer to the hon. member (Mr. Macdonald), that the motion of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll) is now in reality only a notice of motion, no motion has been made at all; and the rule applies to a motion. The bill has been appointed for consideration by the words of the Speaker: "When shall the bill be read a second time?"-and the answer thereto: "At the next sitting of the House." That is the appointment for the consideration of the bill by this House, and consequently a motion cannot be made to deal with the subject matter of it. I only wish to say, so far as the question of technicalities goes, that there is no need for any interference with the rules of the House. All that- has to be done is for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), representing the government on the subject, to move the second reading of the bill, get into committee ,and move all the amendments he desires. But his present action is merely an effort on his part to shift responsibility from the shoulders of the government. If the minister would move the second reading of the bill, the motion could be discussed, the House could go into committee on the bill, the minister could move whatever amendments he liked, and two discussions might thus be avoided.

I have the right
also to refuse to do what my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) suggests. Here in my hand is a copy of the bill I introduced, and which I can send across to my right hon. friend if he desires; in it there will not be found a single reference to oleomargarine. I gave an assurance to the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) and also the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll) that the bill would not contain anything on that subject, and yet I find another bill on the order paper apparently prohibiting the manufacture of oleomargarine. Why should I not exercise my right to discharge this order and re-draft the bill?

That must be by unanimous consent. The Speaker is the servant of the House and at the same time he must be guided by the rules established by custom, by precedent and by law. The House can at any time take upon itself to suspend the rules, but the Speaker being the servant of the House, and being bound by the rules, can only cite them in support of his rulings.

May I ask the minister a
question? I understood him to say that the bill he introduced had no reference to oleomargarine. I have here Bill No. 186 which does refer to oleomargarine. Are there two bills under consideration?

Order. I think this discussion has lasted long enough. A few moments ago, when the point of order was taken, I intimated that I inclined to the view

that the hon. member could not proceed with his motion whilst the same subject matter was regularly on the order paper before the House. I have listened to the remarks made on both sides, and I still hold the same opinion, that if the motion was proceeded with it would "anticipate a matter already appointed for consideration by the House," such as the subject matter of the bill introduced by the Minister of Agriculture. The case is exactly in point and I am deciding according to parliamentary practice.
Let me remind hon. members that, technical as the objection may at first sight seem to be, and arbitrary as the rules may sometimes appear-and I do not wish to lecture hon. members-these rules are the result of centuries of deliberation. When one studies them every day, as I do, one finds that there is a profound philosophy in, and a raison d'etre for, each and every rule governing our parliamentary procedure. They were enacted for the protection of the people and of parliament as well.
Coming back to the point of order, I affirm my ruling that this debate cannot be proceeded with this afternoon because there is on the order paper a matter already appointed for consideration by the House, similar to that contained in the motion made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
Ocean and river service-investigation into wracks, $12,300.

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry that I could not be present the other evening to hear the last part of the speech of my hon. friend from Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill). He has imposed upon himself a great deal of work in connection with
4 p.m. the investigation into the wreck of the Alaskan on the Pacific coast, and he is to be commended for the great interest he has taken in this matter. I shall carefully examine and consider the evidence which was brought before the Commissioner of Wrecks and the assessors, and their report thereon together with the remarks of my hon. friend.
As far as the Commissioner of Wrecks is concerned, I desire to say that his main function is to find out whether the master or other officers are at fault in the loss of their

Supply-M arine and Fisheries
ship. During the course of the investigation there was nothing to show that the unfortunate men who lost their lives in that wreck were in any way responsible for the disaster. However, I promise my hon. friend that if the evidence adduced points to the fact that the owners neglected to comply with any of the laws and regulations governing shipping-for instance, if they failed to report the condition of the machinery of the Alaskau -instructions will be given for the necessary steps to be taken to bring them before the proper tribunal.
With regard to changing the mode of holding these investigations, and the suggestion of my hon. friend that an Admiralty judge could discharge the duties much more satisfactorily, I may say that masters, mates and pilots would be the first to protest against such a change. They claim that these investigations can be much better conducted by men of the craft, men who have had practical experience in seamanship and who know the difficulties which have to be overcome on the high seas. There is much to be said in support of their contention; and the fact that the investigator is a certificated master and has to be assisted by two assessors, also certificated masters, would seem to me to ensure a thorough investigation in all cases. Of course, mistakes may be made. However, the argument of my hon. friend will be fully considered. I think he has made a strong case for reducing the tonnage of vessels subject to inspection so far as the hull is concerned. This matter has been brought to my attention by my hon. friend personally many times, and I am free to admit that I have been rather impressed by the arguments he has put forward to obtain that change. The law we have now has been in force since 18S2. Inspection is required for vessels over 150 tons, and of course, all passenger vessels whatever their tonnage must be inspected. There are objections, coming especially from the owners of the smaller boats, which are very numerous, as my hon. friend knows. There may be objections so far as the expense which the change would involve is concerned, but that is of secondary importance. It is my intention that there shall be a full revision of the Shipping Act next year, and this question will be one of those which will engage the attention of the government, and I can assure my hon. friend that his arguments will be given all the consideration they deserve.
As regards the question of clearing up the trail on the west coast and replacing the bridges, I shall be pleased to confer with
my colleague the Minister of Public Works and try and get what my hon. friend has asked for in the matter.
So far as the life-saving improvements are concerned, I have already announced what was the intention of ,the department, and I am pleased to see that my hon. friend has declared himself satisfied with the programme we have in view.

Item agreed to.
Navigation schools, $8,000.

I should like to bring to the attention of the hon. minister the matter I spoke of last year, the remuneration which is paid to men like Captain Marshall O'Hara who are conducting schools for master mariners. I think I brought to the attention of the minister last year what an excellent officer Captain O'Hara was, and I prayed the minister to be good enough to consider the advisability of giving him an increase in salary. I should like to ask if that has been done.

Captain O'Hara is now receiving 81,860 a year, or S155 monthly. Of course, I should be pleased if there was an opportunity to increase his salary. I may say that there are many officers and employees of the department for whom increases are asked, but I find difficulty in increasing the amount of my estimates both in council and in parliament.

I am not criticizing the hon, minister in regard to that. I know there are many demands for increases of salary, but my impression is this, coming from a race of sea-faring men; "They that go down to the sea in ships, they that do business in great waters", as the Bible says, are not, in my opinion, getting adequate remuneration for services. It is all very well to ask for increases in a department where a great number of those concerned are landlubbers looking after the rights of master mariners and sailors. All I have to ask is that the sailor of this country get adequate return for the work that he gives. I represent a constituency which in days gone by built the largest sailing vessels in the world and produced some of the greatest mariners in the world, and I would like to see more men of that type in the minister's department.
My hon. friend may be sure that his representations will be fully considered.

What salary does Captain Eddy receive, at Vancouver?

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
Captain Eddy is Supervising Examiner of Masters and Mates and gives lectures as well in the navigation school. His salary, which comes under another item, is $2,580.
Where are these schools?
At Halifax, Yarmouth, North Sydney, St. John, Quebec, Kingston, Collingwood, and Vancouver.
Is $1,000 given to each?

No. Some of them run the year round, and others only for some months each year. The salaries paid vary according to the length of time these men are engaged. In Halifax and Yarmouth the instructors give their whole time; in North Sydney four months; in St. John their whole time; in Quebec four months; and I think it is whole time in Collingwood and Vancouver.
I suppose a study of the principles of navigation and of the chart and compass is carried on at these schools?
It is to provide instruction for seafaring men who want to qualify as masters and mates. Afterwards they have to pass their examinations for certificates as officers.
Is this all that they cost Canada-just $8,000?
For these schools, yes.
I mean the training for masters and mates. This is all the Dominion pays for education of this kind?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
To provide for the temporary relief of distressed seamen, pay legal expenses and the cost of shipping books and forms, $5,000.
The minister has some resolution on the order paper about this, too. What is the relationship between the resolution and this vote?

This appropriation is to provide for the relief of destitute or otherwise distressed seamen in foreign countries and bring them home. The resolution on the order paper is applicable only to sailors working on Canadian ships.
Then I would think the minister could reduce this estimate if previously it has taken care of all of them.

It has not always, because I see that in 1921-2 the expenditure was $15,991. We cannot fix a definite amount because it depends on the wrecks that occur and the number of people who may have to be helped out of this appropriation.

Was it formerly the case that the master of a wrecked vessel when taken to a foreign port could not be sent home at the expense of the Canadian people? The sailors were looked after, but I understand the master mariner could not be sent home at the expense of the Dominion. As I understand it, under the present resolution masters may be treated in the same way as sailors.
I do not know that any distinction was ever made in this respect between masters and seamen.

I might say, with all deference to the minister, the old rule was that the master of a ship was not in any way helped home. In the old days the sailors were taken charge of and sent home, but a master could not be returned to this country at the expense of Canada. I know that was the case, from facts within my own personal knowledge.
It may have been the practice, but there was nothing in the law to warrant differentiation in treatment as between masters and men.
Is that practice followed now? It is a bad practice.
It has not been followed of late.

The master of a ship can claim from the owner of the ship the right to be brought home and to be helped in case of sickness, or any other difficulty he gets into. The sailors cannot do that, as I understand it.

Item agreed to.
Removal of obstructions in navigable waters, $5,000.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Does this apply to the wrecks of sunken vessels?
Yes, it is especially for that purpose.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
Does the department undertake to remove the wrecks of sunken vessels in navigable waters in all cases, or is the unfortunate owner required to pay the cost of the removal?

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
We always try to recover from the owners the amount which the department has spent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip
speechtext: I may point out that very often great hardship is worked in such cases. Very frequently men are engaged in the coasting trade when that employment is not very remunerative and when the vessels are without any insurance. In such cases if the master loses his vessel it seems to be an additional hardship to call upon him to pay for the cost of removing the wreck. I have one or two cases in mind, and I am glad to have the assurance of the minister that the department is prepared to pay the cost where the owner cannot afford to do so himself.

As a matter of fact, the usual custom is for the department to do the work and recover from the owners. The department has to see that the obstructions are removed as quickly as possible. In such cases we must pay the men we employ and we try to recover from the owners afterwards.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip
speechtext: I have in mind now a case where a vessel was lost in the mouth of a river in Prince Edward Island. That wreck is at the bottom, but the department has informed the unfortunate owner that he has to maintain a buoy there as a protection to [DOT]other vessels that might encounter the obstruction. That is a continuing cost upon [DOT]the owner that he can very ill afford to pay. I should like very much if the minister would take that case into consideration, and I will bring it to his attention later on. '
I certainly will.

Under this heading I should like to ask the minister if adequate measures are taken for the protection of navigation. This vote provides for the removal of obstructions. But we had lately the case of the wreck of the Marvale. What provisions are made in the shape of wireless equipment and other means to prevent that kind of thing? As I understand it is easily possible now for any vessel to ascertain exactly where it is in a fog. Devices were perfected during the war which enabled ships in the North Sea in a dense fog to tell their exact position. So that the wreck of the Marvale off the coast off Cape Race might easily have been prevented if the proper precautions had been taken. Is there an efficient wireless service there so that a vessel can ascertain its location? If not, I should like to know from the
minister if some improvements could not be made in this direction for the protection of shipping in those foggy areas around Cape Race and the shores of Newfoundland.

I have no objection to answer my hon. friend now, though the matter will come up later under another item. In the specific case to which my hon. friend has referred if its position had been asked for by the Marvale it could have been given. All the necessary facilities exist for that purpose. There is a direction-finding station at Cape Race quite in the vicinity where this accident occurred. The station was in full operation and we are fully convinced that its direction could have been given to the Marvale.
Then, do I understand the minister to indicate that the wreck of the Marvale was a case of neglect on the part of the master?
I do not say that. What I say is that the facilities for giving the directions to the vessel were there.
I see, and he did not take sufficient precautions to ascertain through those facilities where he was.

He never asked the
officers in charge of the station.

I should like to call the attention of the minister to an obstruction in Seymour Narrows on the east coast of Vancouver Island. There is a rock there which is something like ten feet below the surface at low water, and there is a strong tide which runs at the rate of nine or ten miles an hour through the strait. The result is that the passage is made very dangerous for vessels passing through. While there is a good width of water on the east side the danger is very much increased because there is a channel on one side, also with a very swift current, which tends to drive the boats over to this rock. It was only a year or two ago-possibly two or three years now-when one of the big American boats-because this is in the direct line of travel from Seattle to Skagway-was coming down and the current carried the stem in and she struck this rock knocking a hole in her bottom. Fortunately, they were able to beach the steamer about a mile and a half or a couple of miles further down, and by that time she had practically sunk, otherwise there would have been a total loss of life. It is calculated it would only cost four or five thousand dollars to blow this rock up. It consists of two pin-



Supply-Marine and Fisheries
nacles and it would not cost a great deal to blow them up. This would mean safety of navigation to the vessels taking that route. If this is not done there is going to be a big disaster there some day, because the boats that follow that route may be carried away by this current and driven over on to this rock. I think some of the officials of the department will remember the disaster referred to. I do not recall the name of the boat. Had she not been beached in the way I have described the whole of her passengers would have been lost.

The suggestion of my hon. friend would not come under this item, not even under this department. This item deals only with obstructions caused by wrecks or sunken vessels. The removal of this rock would come under the Department of Public Works, but I shall be pleased to submit the remarks of my hon. friend to my colleague.
I thought perhaps the Minister of Marine and Fisheries might prove more generous than the Minister of Public Works.

Item agreed to.
Inspection of * live stock shipments, $3,000.

I presume this is the work carried on, according to the Minister of Agriculture, by Mr. Duncan Marshall, and we can discuss that subject. What is meant by inspection of live stock by the Marine department?

This item was in the estimates prior to Mr. Duncan Marshall being discussed in the Canadian parliament. This appropriation is for the purpose of defraying costs incurred in the inspection of live stock for shipment in vessels, as provided by chapter 130, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906. , Under that act ships carrying live stock cannot clear from port without a government inspection certificate. The additional $500 required for 1923-4 as compared with 1922-23 is to provide for the salary and expenses of an inspector at the port of St. John, N.B.-part time-and for salary increases for two inspectors at the port of Montreal.

It has been suggested to the minister that he should consider combining the work of inspection with the Department of Agriculture. We are told that we are going to have all our live stock shipments inspected by that department. Therefore, we should get rid of overlapping which seems to be unnecessary. Most of the information covered by the certificate is

purely formal, and does not amount to anything at all, such as the seaworthiness of the boat and that sort of thing, because all that is looked after particularly in connection with passenger boats; so that the inspection of live stock should be dealt with by the Department of Agriculture.

WTith the expansion
which agriculture will take under the new regulations, I think the suggestion of my hon. friend might be accepted.

Item agreed to.
To continue subsidies for wrecking plants-Quebec and British Columbia, $35,000.
Are these under the supervision of the Department of Marine?
Yes.
How much was spent last year?
We spent the entire amount: $25,000 to the Quebec Salvage and Wrecking Company Limited, and the other $10,000 to the Pacific Salvage Company Limited, on the western coast.
Is that by contract or services rendered?
Contract.
What work was done by the Quebec company last year?
The company salvaged $47,766 last year.

How many
wrecks did they look after?
Ten wrecks in the Quebec district.
Is the wrecking contract given as the result of a tender, or how?

It was renewed. They are the only people who possess the necessary plant for that purpose. The contract was renewed twice, I understand, for five years, and it was renewed again last year for a similar period.

Item agreed to.
Unforeseen expenses, $5,000.
How much was the amount spent last year?
It was $4,202.

What were the unforeseen items?

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

This is for expenses
which could not be anticipated-legal expenses, criminal investigations!, advice, assistance of experts, and so forth.

Has this item been in for
many years?
Yes.
The same amount?
Yes, $5,000. Last year the expenditure was $4,202 and the previous year it was only $2,186, but the amount asked for was the same.
How much the year before?

I have only the two
years.
Sir HENRY DRAYl'ON: A fair ratio of increased cost with the change of government.

Item agreed to.
Life-saving service, including rewards for saving life, $90,000.
Is this under the minister's department?
Yes.
And it is maintained by the department?
Yes.

It was brought to my attention that the life-saving station near the end of Long Point, Lake Erie, is not in a position to function properly. I have never been there myself, but I am informed that this station is greatly in need of a power boat equipment. It is located on the inside of the point, on the bay side, where no wrecks ever occur, or could possibly occur, because there is no navigation there. It is at least five miles away from the point where any wreck could occur. They are only equipped with a rowboat, and a power boat is needed. I think it would be an advantage to put the life-saving station on the outside of the point where wrecks are likely to occur. As it is at present, a power boat or tug could leave Port Dover and reach any possible wreck just as quickly as the life-saving crew could reach it by rowing there. I think it would be well if the department would look into this, and see if some improvement could not be made regarding this station.

I shall be glad to have
the officers of the department investigate what
213	J
my hon. friend has just said, more so because the station to which he refers is one where we are spending most money in Ontario. The maintenance is at a cost of $7,500 a year, and the others are at much smaller amounts. The amount spent last year to the end of March-that does not include the month of April-is $60,635.96. I mean that some accounts had not reached the department in April.
Does the minister himself decide who is to obtain money for saving life? That is, are awards made, or are these amounts merely for maintenance of the stations?
This is for maintenance of stations on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts and on the Great Lakes.
Are any rewards paid?

Yes. The appropriation covers rewards for saving life on the high seas where exceptional bravery is shown and risks taken in rescues. These rewards are made to the crews of Canadian vessels making rescues or the crews of other lines who rescue lives from danger. Of course claims for such rewards are investigated by a branch of the department.
How much was paid for claims in that channel alone?
I am afraid I cannot give my right hon. friend that information now.
Is an order in council required for approval of a recommendation for the payment of a reward for life-saving, or does the minister dole out the money himself?

If the amount is small,, the minister deals with the matter himself-That has always been the practice. But if the amount is a little large, the matter goes through the formality of an order in council.
No order in council is then legally necessary. I should like to know about how much is paid in this case, because this is really an extraordinary power.
I am informed that it is possible that no money at all was paid last year for any reward of that kind, but I could not say that positively. I will try to get the information for my right hon. friend.
Item agreed to.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
Hydrographic Survey and to provide for the maintenance and repairs of hydrographic steamers, $364,080.
I was wondering whether this is a work that needs to be repeated every year, whether it is maintenance work. Will the work ever be done and this amount decreased?

This is to provide for the continuation of surveys by ship parties on the Atlantic coast, in the lower St. Lawrence and on the Pacific coast, and by small land parties in harbours and sheltered localities ; the maintenance of automatic gauges on the St. Lawrence and Great Lakes and the compilation of charts and other similar work in the nature of aids to safe navigation in Canadian waters. It is new work that is going on. There are a few vessels which are especially engaged in this work under a branch of the department under Mr. Stewart.
Is the increase due to statutory increases?

The increase of $14,080 is to provide for certain necessary repairs and renewals of plant and equipment. It is also proposed to keep the steamer Acadia in commission for the work of ice-breaking operation on the south-eastern coast of Nova Scotia. That will involve some additional expenditure.

On every boat that one sails on, they have to-day apparently the most perfect charts showing, not only every indentation and every rock, but a photograph of the surface of the water. These all seem to be very old, indicating that the variations, shiftings since, have not been very great. I ireally would think it was not necessary to maintain so expensive a service as this costing ^between a quarter and half a million dollars -a year.
Still, we cannot grant all the demands which are made upon the department for new surveys.
You could never do that.
There are some especially for British Columbia at the present time. A large part of our coast has not been properly surveyed for the safety of navigation so far.

It seems very strange
to me. I do not know anything they do not know; I have never heard any complaint that there was any uncertainty as to the character of the coast line or of the floor of the ocean. Is it not just possible that the primary incitement to more expenditure

comes from those who get the money, and they utilize others to serve their own ends? That is the case in many parts of the service.	,

I may give my hon.
friend a resume of the work which it is intended to do this year.
As regards the Pacific coast survey, the main work in hand on the Pacific coast is a survey of the waters off the southwest of Aristazabel and Banks islands in the southeast entrance to Hecate strait, as well as the completion of the surveys of Seaforth channel and Lama passage. The fine weather of the season from about the middle of June to the beginning of September will be used for this work. During the earlier part of the season and the autumn months operations will consist of sounding in the entrances to Victoria and Esquimalt, a re-sweeping of First narrows, Victoria harbour, and surveys of Genoa bay, Perceval narrows, Port Black-ney, Laredo channel, Surf and Cumshewa inlets. For this work the steamer Lillooet and the small tug Restless will be available.
As regards the Atlantic coast survey, as soon as the Acadia has finished fitting out she will be stationed off the west coast of Nova Scotia at the approach to the Bay of Fundy and will continue the off-shore sounding started last season, when the work showed considerable necessity for new soundings. Next winter it is proposed that she continue breaking ice for the harbours of the southeast coast of Nova Scotia.
As regards the Lower St. Lawrence surveys, the party on the Cartier will, during the coming season, work in the southwest approach to the channel north of Anticosti island where traffic has greatly increased during the last few years and through which more information, both as regards hydrography and magnetic declination, is urgently required.
As regards the Magdalen island survey, the steamer Bayfield has been thoroughly overhauled during the past winter and will take up again the work of charting the waters in the vicinity of Magdalen islands, which had to be discontinued during 1922 on account of the condition of the steamer.
As regards the St. Lawrence river, it is proposed to undertake an examination of the river from end to end for the purpose of locating recent improvements, buoys, lights and conspicuous marks to furnish necessary information for a revision of the present charts. This is a work that has to continue almost permanently.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

Exactly at what time
did the Canadian authorities take over this work from the Imperial authorities? For a great number of years the British authorities kept the cruisers on the Atlantic doing this work and making charts. I do not see them there now? I presume that the Canadian authorities have taken that work over?
I cannot give the exact date when it was done but the Canadian authorities did take it over.
They have taken over a lot of work in that connection.
Yes.
I heard, during the minister's explanation, soft, sweet accents from that vessel the Restless. Is there not a history to that vessel?
This is not the same Restless that my hon. friend has in mind.
I thought I had struck one of the holes out of which this money went. Apparently there is another Restless?
I am afraid I must confess my ignorance of the history of the former Restless.	[DOT]

Oh. However when we get to the right Restless-the	government
seems to be restless on both oceans-I shall have a few words to say about it. Whereabouts in the Estimates will this Restless on the Atlantic coast come in?
Under the Customs estimates.
It is not in my department at all; I was getting restless myself.

Item agreed to.
Radiotelegraph service and to provide for the building and maintenance of wireless stations and the general administration of radiotelegraphy throughout the Dominion, $454,900.

There is a mistake in the printed Estimates. An amount of $22,410 ought to be deducted from the total. Certain items that had originally been included in the vote were struck out in council before the estimates were submitted to the House; hence the mistake. The amount therefore ought to be $432,490, which should give a decrease of $7,910 instead of an increase as shown in the estimates as they appear to the committee.
What was the revenue from licenses last year?

On the east coast the revenue for the fiscal year 1921-22 was $16,931.28; for ten months during the fiscal year 1922-23 it was $2,141.34. The Barrington passage station was closed on August 15, 1922. This station had been opened during the war and was no longer necessary. On the west coast the revenue for the fiscal year 1921-22 was $37,065.93, and for ten months during the following year $28,263.51. On the Great Lakes the revenue in 1921-22 was $164.55; for the following year the figures are not yet available.
I notice there is provision for a building and maintenance for wireless stations. Would not this more properly come under the Public Works department?

Part of the government wireless operations, as a matter of fact, is under the Public Works department still, while there is a branch of it in the National Defence department. But the radiotelegraphic service generally is under the Marine department. The idea is rather to concentrate instead of separating, and I think that all branches of the service will be under the Marine department as soon as this can be conveniently accomplished.

I was referring to the building itself. Why should not this be under the Public Works department, so that we might know how much money was being expended for all buildings? If it were included under the Public Works estimates we could ascertain just how much was being spent for all public buildings, and it would be so much easier to find it all under the estimates of one department.

The building of wireless stations is rather a technical work, and I think my hon. friend will agree that it is better that the technical officers of the Department of Marine, who are specially qualified for this undertaking, should do the work under that department.

I know that the technical equipment must be installed by the special officers of the Marine department, but I was referring to the building itself. However, would the minister inform the committee where the new buildings will be erected?

The amount includes revotes in the sum of $19,500 for additions and alterations to the government system provided Tor last year but which it was considered desirable to hold over for a year. These include the installation of continuous wave-transmitters at Dead Tree point and Digby island. British Columbia, and the erection of

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
a dwelling house at the Canso direction finding station. In addition to this provision is also made for the erection of a direction finding station at a point to be selected on the west coast; for the erection of a direction finding station at St. Paul's island; for the erection of beacon stations at Belle Isle, and Heath Point, Anticosti; for the conversion of the station at Cape Sable into a direction finding station; for the transfer of Cape Bear station to Charlottetown; of the Cape Lazo station at Powell river, and of the Dead Tree Point station to Queen Charlotte city; and for the installation of continuous wave transmitters at Estevan station and Gonzales hill station. There is a net decrease of $7,910 as compared with 1922-23.
This includes salaries?
Yes, everything.
What stations are along the north shore of lake Erie? Is there a station at Port Burwell?
There are stations at Port Arthur, Sault Ste. Marie, Midland, Port Burwell, Toronto, Kingston, and Tobermory. These are the stations in Ontario.

Perhaps the
minister can tell us how much of the vote goes for salaries? That should really be under civil government.
I have not the information here, I am sorry to say. This includes operators' salaries.
Of course it does. I should have thought that my hon. friend would at least have the information of the major part of his estimates.
I thought I was well supplied with information, but obviously this is one respect in which I cannot answer my hon. friend's question.

Can his deputy not turn up the salaries? While my hon. friend's deputy is looking that up-I think he must have the information in that big volume-I should like to know what became of the radiotelegraph bill. I suppose it went through?
Yes.
When the bill was before us the minister told me I could get particulars of the receipts from licenses when this item was under discussion. Can my friend give me this information now?
I think I gave all that information when the bill was before the House on its second reading.

Then I was not
present, because I was told I could get the information when these estimates were up.
I will have a statement prepared and present it after eight o'clock.
Perhaps my hon friend can tell me what has been done under that bill.

The only arrangement made has been with the province of Manitoba. In fact I said at the time the bill was before the House that it was the case of Manitoba which we wanted to meet. The fee for a receiving station was one dollar. We have increased it to two dollars, half of which will go to the province of Manitoba.
If that basis is followed we will have no loss in fees.
No. As a matter of fact the number of receiving stations is increasing daily.

Oh yes. Then there is another matter I intended to bring up when the bill was called, but apparently I was out of the House. Has the minister taken this matter up with the military authorities? We spend a good deal of money on the instruction of signal men, and many people connected with the service are of the view that if these distributing stations were placed in the hands of the men who are being trained in our military camps and the like it would be the most practical way of teaching them. They could do the broadcasting just as well as private individuals and at the same time receive very good instruction. Has that been considered by my hon. friend?
Negotiations are taking place at the present time between .the two departments to that end. But even now a large number of military men are employed in this work.

I suppose the item had better stand until we get the information.	.
Item 227 stands.
Tidal and current survey, $35,000.

What is the difference between this item and No. 226?

The triplication of dredging services, as appears to be the fact, leads one to the conclusion that if considerable saving is to be made in the public service, then we must obtain, so far as government services are concerned, some co-ordinating factor. I remember reading a report of Sir George Murray, written some ten years ago, in which he suggests that it would be a great thing to have co-ordination in the public service. Just at this point I want to suggest that the British Treasury Board has been empowered to do that particular work. Our Treasury Board, as I understand it, is not empowered to undertake the work of co-ordination, not by statute in any event. It seems to me that something has to be done along that line, if a saving is to be effected, and I am positive that that is the method which will result in the saving of perhaps hundreds of thousands of dollars to this country every year. I think it is along that line that exploration must be made if we are going to have not only an efficient public service in the country, but also an economical public service.

The sooner an effort is made by every government, no matter what it is, to eliminate patronage entirely from the public service, the better it will be for the country.

I would inform the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) that our provincial government in Manitoba does not exercise any patronage. I am not opposed to the Liberals placing their own friends in positions if there are vacancies and if those friends happen to be qualified and the positions are properly filled under the Civil Service Act. But I do want to assure the hon. gentleman, speaking in the name of my own province, that we have no patronage in Manitoba.
I want to put a thought or two to the member for Dorchester that he can think over in the dinner hour.
I can think it over right now.
The hon. member spoilt his speech, so far as it might have any effect on a fair-minded audience, by the assertion that the Civil Service Commission is a farce.
Under the old government.
Under the late government, yes; that is what the hon. member said. Now, there has been some investigation lately, and there is not a member of this House who would suggest sincerely-
Will you allow me a question?
Certainly.
If the right hon. gentleman intended that the Civil Service Commission should carry out the law as it stands, how is it that the old commissioners were replaced by friends of his?

To start with, they were not replaced by friends of ours. One member of the three on the commission was appointed by the government that preceded us, the Laurier government. The secretary, who has always been known to be most influential and to take an active part in the commission, was also appointed by the preceding govern-{Mr. Shaw.]
ment. All we did was to appoint the other two. I do not know that such a proceeding can be duplicated by the present administration.
Does the right hon. gentleman claim that it is not a matter of patronage to appoint a minister to the Civil Service Commission?
There was no minister appointed.
What about Doctor Roche?
He had been a minister, it is true.
He could not be both at the same time; if it had been possible, he would have taken both, jobs.

I do not think the hon. member gets anywhere by an assertion of that sort, if it is put before any fair-minded man in the Dominion. Hon. members know the present chairman of the commission, and I do not think that anyone will seriously suggest that the commission has acted partisanly in all the time of its existence, either under the late government or under this government. The member who asserts it is a mere partisan instrument does not contribute much to the establishment of the judicial character of the commission, nor does he contribute much to his own reputation in this House. What he states is simply not the fact. I want to say this, however, I have heard the number dismissed by the previous government stated at different times variously: at one time it is 6,000, at another time 8,000, and to-day 12,000. I have no doubt that in a few years it will have risen to 112,000. But one will be as near the truth as the other. Certainly, there were some dismissals and there was debate upon them. But I believe that any hon. member who reads the debates will see that they were not carried to any great extreme; and there was considered to be, as I think there was in some cases, ample justification for certain dismissals. It is true, however, that there was not at that time in the outside service of Canada any pretence at a commission. No government had dared to take that course, and no member of this House can know, unless he was a member of that government that did, what a government will encounter that does dare to take such a step.

Would my hon. friend
agree that I should reinstate in my department all the employees dismissed without investigation in 1912?

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

Dear me! I think if
he would replace all those dismissed in 1896 he would not be going back too far.

Does my hon. friend
say there was an investigation in every case?
There was an investigation. There may not have been an investigation by a commissioner under the Inquiries Act in each case.

Most of the officers in
my department were dismissed without investigation.

If we are to go back
from one election to the other we get nowhere. There can never be reform if you are going to carry on the principle of vengeance; it cannot be done. The hon. gentleman says I was a partisan of the partisans. I venture to suggest to him that I had to do with the appointment .directly of more Liberals than Conservatives. In my own county only one was dismissed. Nor was I a member of the government until the middle of 1913, in fact I was not a member of the Cabinet until 1915. I do not think he was quite justified in pointing to me as the arch-offender in effecting dismissals. Besides, the majority of the appointments I had to do with, which were chiefly to the Bench, were in favour of Liberals.
During the Union Government?

Yes, and Liberals were
appointed who opposed Union government.
Who are they?

One of them was the
son of a recent hon. member opposite who was opposed to Union government throughout. He was appointed by the previous government a judge of the Supreme Court of Saskatchewan.
The exception proves the rule.

Others I could name
one by one. These were much more important offices than the petty ones whose occupants hon. gentlemen opposite have dismissed. Faithful servants, one by one, score by score, have been dismissed. That is not in the interests of those individuals, it is not in the interests of the civil service of Canada. A strong effort has to be made to stand to what we have reached. If we cannot get any farther, let us at least not retrogress. I make that appeal to the government, and I
do so particularly on this item because I think it is in relation to it that the chief transgression has taken place.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We were discussing item 230:
To provide for the maintenance and operating of Sorel shipyard, $125,000.

The hon. minister said that an amount of $35,000 was transferred to this item and that that accounted for the increase In regard to the item from which it was transferred has that $35,000 been deducted therefrom?
It has not. As a matter of fact, it was intended to have a much larger amount for the other item, but council decided to reduce it to make an increase of $35,000 only.
And that amount was transferred to this item?
Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the resolution
carry?
I did not know that item No. 229 carried. I understood it was standing till the minister got certain information.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item 227 is to stand, and items 228 and 229 have been carried.
Item 230 stands till the information comes down.

My hon. friend will be surprised at the extent of the misinformation he has received. The number of permanent employees who were dismissed there is very very small indeed. I think I could count them on the fingers of one hand.
They are mostly on the temporary list, are they not?

They are day labourers.
They are in no way permanent. More than that, as to those day labourers who perhaps have considered themselves as being dismissed or as to whom my right hon. friend has been informed by somebody to that effect other shifts have been put on for fifteen days or three weeks just to give employment to the unemployed in the city of Sorel. That
revised edition

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
was done under the supervision of Mr. Lacouture, the Superintendent of the Sorel shipyards, and a supporter of the former government with the co-operation of the charitable associations of Sorel. I do not want to pose as a philanthropist in the matter at all, but really I do not deserve the criticism that is being made.

If the minister would let this item stand and bring down the information, if it is of the character he describes, I assure him there will be no delay so far as I am concerned when this item is reached again.
What is the information my hon. friend wants? The names of the people put out?
Yes.
There were three or four only.
The information I ask for will be found in Hansard. I asked for it about a quarter to six this evening-the dismissals, and on whose certificate,, and what the nature of the information was.
I can tell my hon. friend as to one man. One man, Morgan, was dismissed, and dismissed for cause because he was the secretary of the Tory organization during the last fight.
Bad man.

Politically, not otherwise, and he was dismissed on the recommendation of Mr. Cardin, the member for that constituency who stated that he was the secretary of the Tory organization and took an active part against him in the last election. I thought that was sufficient ground, and I dismissed him.
That is one.
There are two more. I forget their names-
About two hundred more, according to my information.
-but they were dismissed on the same grounds.
If that is the fact there should be no delay when the item is reached again.
We have been discussing this for over two hours now.
And the information i3 not here.
I have given one third of the information. There are two more I think.
Oh!
That is all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

I have asked the minister to hold this item until we get the information. He admits he has not it here. He cannot get through all his estimates, he is holding one item; why not hold this one? About eight have gone through.
Because we have been discussing this for two hours, and to let the item stand would mean the whole discussion over again.
We will discuss it longer still, then.

I really do not deserve the criticism my hon. friend is making. In fact, I am blamed all the time for keeping his friends in office. That is the blame I am receiving, not what he is ascribing to me now.
I do not dispute that, but does he not see the help I am giving him now against that attack?
I think my hon. friend is not giving any help to his friends whom I am keeping in office.

I am not looking to my friends. I am looking to the country.
Item 230 stands.
Amount required for the construction of one selfpropelling Hopper barge (revote), $54,800.
When was this started?
Last year. It is under construction now.

The contract is for $274,000. It was granted to Canadian Vickers, who were the lowest tenderers.

How much has been
spent?

Two hundred and nineteen thousand dollars had been expended, and the contract is for $224,000-

No, $274,000.

Oh, yes, I have the list here:

Ltd. Lauzon, Levis, P.Q	 $300,000
