The tender of Vickers was $274,000, much by far the lowest.
Did I understand the minister to say the contract price was $274,000?
Yes.
Why was $285,000 required?
That was the estimated cost by the engineers of the department.

Item agreed to.
Agencies-rents and contingencies, $212,000.
The increase of $2,000 there provides for the statutory increases in salary.

How many agencies are
there and where are they located?
There are eight agents located as follows: Nova Scotia, New Brunswick. Prince Edward Island, Quebec, Montreal, Parry Sound, Victoria and Prince Rupert.

Why is it necessary to
maintain a separate agency in the province of Prince Edward Island? That must be a very small territory. It seems to me it could be yoked up with either Nova Scotia or New Brunswick.
That agency covers the northern coast of Nova Scotia and the northern coast of New Brunswick as well as Prince Edward Island and the Magdalen islands.
The New Brunswick agency only covers the Bay of Fundy?

The Bay of Fundy and
as far as Lockeport in Nova Scotia.

What are the agencies for,
what work do they perform?
For placing and maintaining necessary aids to navigation and other work. All the lightkeepers and the vessels employed in placing the buoys are under the control of these agencies.

Item agreed to.
Salaries and allowances to lightkeepers, $650,000.

I should like to ask the
minister if the lightkeepers were given any increase in salaries last year?

No. I must admit that there have been requests for increases in the salaries of the lightkeepers, and their case is deserving of consideration. The only reason for not yielding to these requests is economy and the disinclination of parliament to increase any expenditure at the present time. I may say that my hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Forke) told me that he desired to plead for the lightkeepers when this item came up. The question of increasing salaries is under consideration.

Are these men under the
Civil Service Commission?
The most of them are.
Would they get the customary statutory increase if they were under the Civil Service Commission?
There is a minimum and a maximum salary provided in every class and they are getting it year by year.
Is there any prospect of a reclassification in the near future in response to the demand that was made?
The question is being considered.

These officers are certainly not adequately paid for the work they do. Their duty is to protect navigation and in this work they are engaged from the month of April, you might say, up to the month of October. The salary for part time officers engaged in this work amounts to only about $30 or $35 a moDth. With very few exceptions the amount they receive is only $30, which is wholly inadequate to maintain themselves and their families. They are located in very lonely and isolated spots and I think they should have a little more salary than they are now paid in order to enjoy a fair living. Inadequate payment is not much of an encouragement to efficient work. It may be said that if these men do not want the positions they can resign, but that would not be

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
a fair answer to their request. Other men would take the jobs at insufficient salaries. I would ask the minister to consider the advisability of making a reclassification of these officers in order that they may be a little better paid in the future.
Did the minister state the average salary paid to lighthouse keepers?
There are twenty classes of lightkeepers. In class 1, the minimum is $2,880 and the maximum $3,240. There are 10 lightkeepers in class 1.
What class of lightkeepers would those be?

They are in charge of the most important lights. Those are Cape Race, Belle Isle, Bird Rocks, Pelee passage, Es-tevan point, Pachena, Leonard island, Lan-gara, and Sand Heads. There are 21 lightkeepers in class 2. The salary is from $2,100 to 2,280. There are 56 lightkeepers in class 3, with salaries from $1,560 to $1,740. There are 39 in class 4, with salary from $1,500 to $1,680. There are 13 in class 5 with salary from $1,440 to $1,620. There are 17 in class 6 with salary from $960 to $1,200. There are 32 in class 7 with salary from $840 to $930.
Dispense.
I am giving the details.
There are not going to be any lighthouses on the prairies.
The classes continue until we reach class 19 which relate to the contract lights. In class 19 the minimum is $60 and the maximum $80.
Is that per month?
Per annum.
What do they do for that wage?
Those are small wharf lights.
Are the keepers supposed to stay there?
No; they go and light up in the evening and go in the morning to extinguish the lights.
What is the lowest class of full time men and what are they paid?

That would be class No. 7, $840 to $930 per y*ar.
(Mr. Leger.]

I had an interview with one of these gentlemen from my own native country when up here last winter, and he told me he got the magnificent salary of $200 a year. He had been on the job for twenty years. He was appointed by the old government prior to 1911. He further told me it was impossible for him to do any outside work, except once in a while, when he did a little fishing. He also told me he could not possibly live on the salary.
He could not.

And I quite agreed with him. I think this case ought to receive special consideration. This man does the classifying of the lights. Is that under the department? I do not suppose the Civil Service Commission do it.
It was done by the Civil Sendee Commission.
Arthur Young and Company.
No, Griffenhagen.
Possibly the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) thinks he could do it a great deal better himself, but I did not ask him.
I could do it better than the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson).
I take issue on that.
The hon. member would take issue on anything.
Is there an allowance in addition to the salary? This item says, "salary and allowance".
They got a living bonus for the last two years, in common with all other civil servants.
That covers the allowance.
That is not an allowance.
That is not an allowance.

I understand the minister is a little diffident about increasing the salaries because of possible objection by the House. We might appropriate Duncan Marshall's salary and distribute it amongst these men.
Is the salary of $840 for seven months' or twelve months' service?

In many cases it is for twelve months' service.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

I met some of those men from the lighthouses and discussed the whole situation with them, the wages they were getting, the hours they were putting in, the loneliness of their lives, the disadvantage in not being able to educate their children and a great many things. I think really they ought to get a little more pay than they are getting at the present time. I am just as much for economy as any one, but I would like to begin at the top and come down.

I am glad the hon. member takes that view. I know the work that the lighthouse keepers are doing on the St. Lawrence, and I know that in many cases their salaries are not commensurate with the services they give to the country. The employees who deserve the first consideration are the lighthouse keepers.

Could the minister tell us
in what class the Gannett Rock light keeper in the Bay of Fundy is placed?
Could the minister increase the salaries of the lighthouse keepers without going to the Civil Service Commission?
No, they have been classified.

There is no light on
Gannett Rock.
Yes, I have been there myself.
Are any of these lighthouse keepers provided with a house?

All the permanent ones,
the full-time men have houses.

Item agreed to.
Maintenance and repairs to lighthouses, $850,000.
Has the maintenance any reference to food, or do these men supply their own food?
This increase has reference to fuel, delivery and supply, freight and cartage, for the use of the staff.
Are these purchases by tender or by agents of the department?
In every case by tender and contract, except for small merchandise requirements?
How many lighthouses has the department to keep up?
The minister said supplies were purchased by tender. Is there a public advertisement for these supplies, or is there a selected list in each case.

We ask prices from the
dealers in every locality.

The minister asks the
friends of the government to put in tenders?
No.
I understand there are no public tenders called for in the province of New Brunswick.

No more in New Brunswick than elsewhere. We are asking the dealers for prices of articles in the different localities. Tories and Grits are invited to give their prices, and in many cases the friends of my hon. friends get the contract.

Is the minister quite sure
of that?

Yes, there have been
many changes in this country.

That is why the minister
is1 where he is.

I wish to draw the attention of the minister to an item which seems to have been neglected by the agent in the district. I refer to a very important light on the mainland, at Richibucto Cape. I understand the keeper has asked the agent to look after it and get it put in proper shape, but it has not been done. Some complaint was made last year. This place is open from the shore right up to the light and the cattle go in. The agent paid no attention to the complaint and it has' not been remedied. Therefore, I call the attention of the minister to it so that he may see that the matter will be attended to in the future,

The hon. member is not the only member who is in such a position. There are many others. We are asking for repairs of that kind. This vote formerly was $1,000,000, but it has been decreased to $850,000, and the unwillingness to increase the appropriation is responsible for certain necessary repairs, such as those my hon. friend mentioned, not being done, but I will try to meet his views.
It was only $800,000 in 192021.

I mean a few years
ago, especially before the war

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

While this may not be
exactly relevant to this item, I should like to get some information in regard to the tugboat Murray Stewart. Last year there was an appropriation of $100,000 in the estimates to replace the Lambton that was lost in lake Superior in a gale with large loss of life. On that occasion the minister, in making an explanation, stated that no decision had been reached whether a boat would be purchased or one would be built. Later on it was discovered that the minister had purchased from one, Mr. Stewart, a gentleman living in Toronto very close to Mr. M. J. Haney, president of the Port Arthur Shipbuilding Company, a ship called the Murray Stewart. This vessel, I am instructed, was built at Port Arthur some few years ago. I am informed that her hull was new but her machinery was old, having been transferred from some other vessel; that the purchase price paid by the department was some $80,000. I am further advised that that vessel had been sent down from the Great Lakes to the harbour of St. John, not under charter, but in the hands of agents for sale, and that at any time that boat could have been purchased for $25,000. Later on, after the Lamb-ton was lost, friends of the government, including Mr. M. J. Haney and his friend, Mr. Stewart, of Toronto, had this boat transferred from the Port Arthur Shipbuilding Company to Mr. Stewart's name, and they unloaded her on the the Minister of Marine and Fisheries at the sum of $80,000. This boat was intended to replace an icebreaker. I understand that she is absolutely useless for that purpose, and that the $80,000 expended for that purpose might just as well have been thrown away; that this spring boats had to be hired to do in Midland harbour the work that she was designed to do. I should like to have some information about [DOT]this boat other than what has been given in -answer to an inquiry made through the order paper.

I must say that this
boat was to replace the Lambton, as my hon. friend has said, and an appropriation of $100,000 was voted last year for that purpose. The department was in immediate need of a boat for the work which had to be performed by her. Only three boats which were suitable for that purpose were offered to the department. They were visited and inspected by the engineers of the department.
What are their names?
I cannot give the names just now.
The deputy will know.

The Murray Stewart
was recommended to me by the officers of the department as being the one best suited for the purpose. It is a steel tug, length 119 feet, beam 26 feet, gross tonnage 234-46, registered tonnage 92 25, speed 11 knots. It was built in 1918 by the Port Arthur Shipbuilding Company, complete except for the engine, which was rebuilt at the time of the construction of the hull. She was purchased for $80,000 from James Frederick Martin Stewart, of Toronto, to replace the Lambton which was lost on lake Superior in the spring of 1922. The boat will also be used to render assistance to ships handling grain in Georgian bay ports at the close of navigation each year. Although she is not intended for an icebreaker, she is much more suited for that work than the one she has replaced.

That may be true, but
if she was purchased for an icebreaker sha could not perform that duty.
She never was purchased for an icebreaker.

That was the explanation
given by the minister last year.
To assist ships in handling grain.

I think I can refer the
minister to the pages of Hansard. Is it not a fact that the engines in this boat were second-hand engines taken out of another boat, and that when she was purchased she had no engines?
' Mr. LAPOINTE:	The engines were in
excellent condition, although second-hand.

That, of course, is not
answering my question.
I said "although secondhand."

I beg pardon. Did the
minister see Mr. Haney in regard to the purchase from Mr. Stewart? If he had any correspondence with him, I would be glad >f he would produce it.

I do not know the
gentlemen. I would not recognize them anywhere if I saw them

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

The minister surely does
not say that he has never met Mr. Haney who laboured for the government down in the Maritime provinces?

I am sorry. My hon.
friend is better acquainted than I am with him. I do not know him.
He has a good name, anyway.

Is this vessel equipped
with wireless?
No, it is not.

Are the other vessels
presently on the Great Lakes equipped with wireless??

None of them on the
Great Lakes.
Why not? The Minister will remember that last fall there was :& great difficulty in regard to navigation on lake Superior. Would it not be well to have these vessels equipped with wireless?

The suggestion is one
which deserves consideration.

More than that, I think
it deserves very favourable consideration. I think all these vessels should be equipped with wireless, especially in view of the situation as it was last fall and as it may be any *other season on the Great Lakes.

That is right, but there
was no wireless there two or three years ago any more than there is now. I have been *trying to keep expenditures down.

May I be excused for
*saying that that is not absolutely in accordance with the facts. The Simcoe was equipped with wireless until she was taken down during the war for service on the ocean.

The Lambton was not
equipped with wireless.
Coming back to the Murray Stewart, I understand that the minister had this boat thoroughly inspected before he bought it?
Yes.
Did the minister dot have to have substantial repairs made on that vessel this last spring-to the boilers?
Some repairs were made on that boat.
After she had been inspected and purchased and $80,000 paid over?
Yes, the $80,000 represented the price of the boat as she was when we bought her.

I agree. What repairs
were put on her and were tenders asked for those repairs?

I may inform my hon.
friend that this boat cost over $200,000 to build.

This boat was built by
the Port Arthur Shipbuilding Company in their own plant. They transferred into her an old engine that had seen years of service, an engine that was in no sense modem. That is one of the reasons why she was not sold when she was down on the Atlantic coast. If she cost $200,000, it must be borne in mind that she was built during the war at the peak of prices, and that is no criterion at all of her value to-day. If the minister doubts that statement he can just consider the merchant marine.
I am not responsible for the merchant marine.
But you are responsible for this vessel.
He wants you to broaden out.

Though I have the
greatest opinion of my hon. friend I must confess that when it is necessary to purchase another boat for my department I shall rather take the advice of the chief engineers and other experts of the department than that of the hon. member.
Of course, that is a very cheap remark to make.
But very appropriate.
But it does not make me subside for a moment.
Oh, no, I do not want to do that.
I should like to know when this boat was taken over, where the crew came from, what was the cost of getting her to the scene of operations, and how long it took to get her there.

My hon. friend should not be over-inquisitive about this item, and I will tell him why: It was passed days ago. I do not object, of course, to his asking any questions in reference to the item, even although it has been already voted, so long
Supply-Marine and Fisheries

as they are reasonable; but he must not overstep the limit. I am quite willing to give all the information I have by me, but this matter does not come under this item.

If the minister has not the information I cannot expect him to give it. But do I understand that when we give him a blank cheque, as we did last year, we are never to ask any questions with relation to the expenditure of the money so voted?
Not at all.

Well, that is what it
amounts to.
The hon. gentleman misinterprets the minister.
My hon. friend gave me a blank cheque of $100,000 for the purchase of a boat; I made a good bargain and got one for $80,000, saving $20,000.
You got a second-hand $25,000 boat for $80,000.
It was built in 1918.

The hull was bu'lt in
1917.
If the repairs cost over $20,000 it might not be a good bargain. The deputy minister is probably trying to find out what the repairs cost.
I cannot tell my hon. friend how much was paid for repairs. I was not supposed to answer these questions to-night, because the item to which they relate has already been passed.
Of course, if the minister takes that stand then it ends the matter.
No, the matter is not necessarily ended; I am simply giving the reason for my not having any information to offer hon. gentlemen in reply to these questions.
I am not finding fault at all with the minister; I am only asking for information if it can possibly be got.
I shall be pleased to get the information.
Then I understand that at the moment the minister cannot tell us what was paid for repairs?
No.
I thought the deputy was looking it up.
So he is, but he has not been able to find it.

Is it not a fact that the boat was intended, among other things, to be used as an ice-breaker, and that she failed to function as such and the department had to hire other boats to do this class of work?
No.
That is my information. Mr. BUREAU: Misinformed again.
Was this boat used for placing the lightkeepers at the respective stations this spring? If not, was she engaged elsewhere, or was she considered unsuitable for the -work?

The ice conditions this >
ear were particularly bad. There was so much ice that it was thought advisable to charter a boat to do the work.
I take it, then, that this boat was not used because she was not equipped to stand the ice.
There was so much ice that it was thought dangerous to use her.
Where can we find the item that provided for the cost of repairs to this boat?
It will be found under Dominion Steamers, item 215.

I would impress upon the minister the necessity for equipping all boats of the merchant marine with wireless.
, Mr. LAPOINTE: I shall certainly take the suggestion into consideration.

What are the regulations governing the closing down of lighthouses in the fall months? Is there a regular date for closing them down, or do they stay open until the navigation companies decide to discontinue operations?
Navigation is supposed to close on December 20, when the lighthouses are closed.
Last year, I know, navigation was open on the Great Lakes after the 20th of December, and the lighthouse keepers were not taken off until some time subsequently.

Navigation closes at the date I have stated, and the lighthouse keepers are picked up as soon as weather conditions permit.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
I know that navigation was open last year a good deal later than it has been in previous years.
The official date is December 20.

I presume it would be easy for the minister to have his deputy turn to the items that make up the total of $1,500,000 referred to in item 215. If he did that we could find out what was required for the repairs of the boat in question.
The repairs to the hull and engine for the year were $11,000.
Was there a tender?

Item agreed to.
Salaries and disbursements of fishery officers and guardians, fisheries patrol and fishery protection services, $880,000.

May I ask the minister if any decision has been reached with respect to the use of Canadian Atlantic ports by American fishermen? That is a live question I think, at the moment, and the House is entitled to a statement with respect to it.
The question is ,still under consideration and a decision will be arrived at shortly. I will then be pleased to make an announcement.
That is the statement that has been given out to the press every day for about ten days.
I am afraid that in most instances the press merely guessed at it.
Well, they are good guessers. The government is doing nothing as usual.
At the last election they were bad guessers.

Not down in my locality. Perhaps the minister, for the information ot the House will state how this question has arisen and what has been the action of the American government as regards the use of their ports?

During the war there was an international commission which investigated all matters concerning the fisheries of both countries, that was one of their recommendations, and it was agreed upon by both governments. The United States ports were opened to Canadian fishing vessels just as the Canadian ports were opened to the American fishing vessels. When the war was over the Americans closed their ports again claiming that the privilege previously enjoyed had been granted under war legislation and that the powers of their War Times Measures Act had expired. On the other hand we kept our ports open to American vessels. Since 1888, under what was called the modus vivendi, American vessels were allowed the use of our ports on payment of a small license fee. Many interests in our country were in favour of granting that privilege to the Americans. Many of our people in the Maritime provinces were selling their fish to Americans.
Did the modus vivendi include a supply of bait as well?

Yes, it did. On the other hand it resulted in placing the Canadian fishermen in a state of inferiority compared to American fishermen, because the latter used our ports for all the purposes mentioned and shipped their fish to the United States in bond and free of duty. Now a very high duty has been imposed on Canadian fish entering the United States under the new Fordney tariff. Consequently there has been a movement on the part of Canadian fishermen to deprive their competitors in the United States of the right which they do not want to grant to our fishermen. Under the conditions as they exist to-day my own opinion is that if we cannot get from the United States privileges similar to those we grant, it is only fair and just that we should treat American fishermen as Canadian fishermen are treated by the United States.

Let me say to the minister that I entirely agree with the concluding part of his observations. You will never gain anything from the American government by lying down and submitting to them; you always want to have something that you car retaliate with in dealing with them. When they closed their ports to our fishermen a mistake was made in not immediately closing our ports to them, regardless of the objection that might be raised by a few supply men in some of the Atlantic ports. If that had been done long ago the United States would have realized that we had a stiff backbone and that we were able to stand up for our own rights. There has been so much delay that the closing of our ports to American fishermen may not have the result my hon. friend anticipates. However, I would say close them at once as far as I am concerned.

I would concur in the statement of the hon. member (Mr. Hanson). As a representative from the Pacific coast, I think it is about time that Canada should treat American fishermen in a manner corresponding to the treatment our fishermen receive over there. I think this government should take a very strong stand on the matter. They should close the Canadian ports to American fishermen, and keep them closed until the ports of the United States are opened to the fishermen of this country.

Building fishways and clearing rivers, $40,000.

When this item was up last year I drew the attention of the minister to the fact that there are two or more dams built across Salmon river in Victoria county with no fishways in them. On that occasion the minister told me the matter had been investigated and it had been found there was not water enough in this river to enable salmon to get up. I made it my business to investigate the question during the recent summer and at a dry period of the season. I was somewhat surprised to find, after the statement of the minister, that this is quite a large river-in fact lumber is driven down it, I believe, for a matter of sixty miles. There is no time in low water when there is not plenty of water for salmon or for boats, and pretty good navigation. The river got its name from the fact that it was teeming with salmon at one time; therefore it was called Salmon river, and is a tributary of the St. John riier, not far below Grand Falls. Salmon cannot go up the Grand Falls in the St. John river. That is one of the reasons why the fish should be able to go up the Salmon river to the breeding ground in the northern country. It was one of the most prolific sources of salmon in years gone by, as I learned from residents whom I interviewed there.

Are there any salmon
there now?

I doubt if there are;
the dams have stopped them coming up. I would, therefore, urge the minister to have the fishery overseer go there and make an inspection.
How long have the dams been there?

I do not know the
number of years. I know there has been quite an urge from the settlers that fishways should be put in the dams when they were built. This was not done, and due to that fact the salmon have become almost exterminated on the upper reaches of the river. If fishways were put in, they could go up there and breed.
There is another matter which I called attention to last year, and I would like some information in regard to it. It is the question of the pollution of the rivers by sawdust from the sawmills. The northern end of the St. John river is the boundary line between the United States and Canada, running through Madawaska county on the one side, and the state of Maine on the other. With regard (Mr. McBride.]
to our own mills on the Canadian side, and in fact on both sides of the river from Grand Falls down, which is Canadian, the regulations are very strict, and well enforced, I believe, by the fisheries overseers to prevent sawdust being dumped into the river, because it is very injurious to the fish. However, there are mills on the American side of the St. John river where the river is a boundary line, and I . believe the sawdust from those mills is being dumped in the river. The American authorities are not very particular about it, because the river almost immediately runs into Canada, and the injury is done in Canada. It is a very great injury. Our Canadian sawmill men are compelled to burn their sawdust, or to carry it back on the high ground where it can do no harm. I suggested to the minister that this matter might be referred to the International Joint Commission. I believe there is such a body, is there not? Has this been done? I asked last year that it should be done, but I believe no action has been taken.

It has been submitted
to the commission, as my hon. friend suggests, and they said it was not a matter they could deal with. We are trying to negotiate with the Commissioner for the state of Maine with regard to this very matter, and I hope we will be able to get a solution such as would suit my hon. friend.
With reference to the hon. member's question in regard to the Salmon river, in view of what he has just said, I will make it a point to send an engineer there this summer to inquire into the conditions, and if it is necessary, we will compel the owners to put in fishways.
Who bears the expense of building these fishways' in the dams? Is it the department or the owners of the dam?
The owners of the dam.

When this matter was up before, I drew the attention of the minister to the fact that there was a little stream up in Manitoba, White Mud river, on which the railway company had a dam near the village of Gladstone. I was assured that the department would look into the matter and see that a fishway was built so that the fish could go up. I understand that during the summer an inspector went up and looked at the dam and the fishway, and from what I caD gather nothing has been done. The citizens there tell me no change has been made. I asked some of the officials of the railway company why they did not fix the slide so that the fish could get up, and they assured me

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
that it was built according to the specifications of the Fisheries department, and they did not know what else they could do. I want to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that a fish inspector going up and looking at the slide does not assist the fish one bit in getting over. We have been trying for a long time to get that fishway built so that the fish could go up. For the last ten or twelve years we have been working at it as hard as we could, and we are no further ahead than when we started. It seems to me it is the next thing to a crime to have in the dams fishways which are not suitable and which the fish cannot climb. It deprives the settlers of the opportunity of getting a few fish in the sipring. If they could get over the dam there is nothing to hinder them going up into the country 40 or 50 miles. Not only that, but the fish die below the dam. They pile up there until they are sticking out of the water, starve to death, and pollute the stream. In addition to that, the fish do not get up to the shallow waters and the sandy beaches to spawn, as I understand they should. I think this is a matter of great importance. It is too bad to have our people deprived of the food, and it is too bad to have the fish depleted, because they cannot go up the river to spawn.

I thought we had written to my hon. friend long ago explaining where the matter stood. We were waiting for the water to subside before taking final action in the matter. It is still engaging the attention of the department, and I hope we shall be able to do something.

We have a fish inspector out in British Columbia whom everybody respects. He simply goes along and when he sees a dam in a creek he gives the owner a certain time to put a passage over it. When the inspector comes back, if the passage is not constructed over the dam as ordered, he blows the whole dam out with dynamite. I do not see why the same regulations should not be enforced in regard to the dam under discussion.
He is an Irishman.
Yes, he is an Irishman,^ and a good one at that.

We are very peaceable and law-abiding on the prairies and do not attempt any such doings as that. The conditions which the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Milne) describes exist all over the prairie, and on the prairies the railway company at intervals have dammed the streams
for the purpose of getting water. I think we brought this matter to the minister's attention last year. I remember some years ago writing to the game guardian in Manitoba complaining that the chutes were so built that the fish could not get up. He inspected them and said that they were built according to law. W'ell, that did not help the fish. I think the trouble is the chutes are so steep that the pike cannot jump over them as the salmon do. The pike are slower going and are unable to get up, except in high water. I agree with the hon. member for Neepawa that while people who are used to salmon, such as the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell), look with contempt upon a pike, we on the prairie are only too glad to get them, because they are good food. It seems a pity that this condition should exist. I know the streams are being depleted. The fish cannot leave the lakes and go up to spawn, and where there were plenty of fish some years ago there is none to-day. My house as almost on the banks of Pipestone creek, and we used to be able to go out and catch a fish any time we wanted to, but we cannot get any now, and the only reason for this is that they cannot spawn. I think the chutes are ,'too steep and the regulations should be altered. The fish cannot go up except in high water. I think the minister might look into this, because it is important.
I would like to impress another matter upon the minister. It is not right for a man to put his own fishway in his dam. He should have someone see that the fishway is properly put in.
Yes.

I can realize why a man running a sawmill with water power does not want a fishway in his dam. It wastes water. He is inclined to put in a small chute that will not waste much water. They had better not waste any water at all if they do not make it big enough so that the salmon can go up.

We always provide
plans and specifications, and an engineer is sent there to see that the work is well done.
We want fair play for the fish.
Does the hon. gentleman suggest that sawdust in a stream does not affect the fish?

I am not suggesting anything of the sort; but with all due respect to my hon. friend, I know as much about fish as he does. I happen to come from a fishing constituency, and I was brought up practically in a fishing boat or vessel. I quite understand that sawdust or other mill refuse, is deleterious to fish life. But when, in order to meet the demands of one or two in a particular community, as regards streams away inland you put injunctions on millers who are making a living by sawing a few boards, you are putting a wrongful injunction upon industry. I am glad the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) is no longer in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and I hope the minister has not many officials with the same views on fish life as the hon. member for Hants has.

is only twenty hours from Boston. If our produce were shipped via Fredericton, which is only 150 miles distant, it would help matters considerably, provided that proper train connections were established. As it is now we are one day and a half from Fredericton but with proper train connections we could land our fish at that point in about nine hours. It would then leave Fredericton in the afternoon, landing in Boston next morning. At that rate the Baie des Chaleurs coast would be twenty-two hours' run from Boston, so that fish from the coast could be placed in the Boston or New York market as the case might be in twenty-two or twenty-four hours instead of after a delay of fifty-six hours as is now the case. This is one matter that the department might look into.
Some time ago an hon. member from Ontario in the Fisheries committee made the statement that at certain times of the year good fish was almost a luxury in some parts of Ontario and could not be bought at any price, whereas our fishermen in the county of Gloucester had dumped on the American markets millions upon millions of pounds of nice fish which they could not sell to cover the freight and tariff charges entirely. This is one respect in which the department could be of some real advantage to the fishermen of that part of the country. I think that we should have proper rail connections, and there should at the same time be established some kind of intelligence bureau that would keep the Maritime provinces in touch with other sections of the country. Fish, it has been proved, is one of the most valuable foods that can be used; and it has been stated that the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island have produced some of the most intelligent men

and I am not speaking of myself for a moment-that this country has seen.
Do not be so modest.

We have contributed
able men to the political life not only of Canada but of the Mother Country. For example, the late Prime Minister of Great Britain, the Right Hon. Mr. Bonar Law, is a native of my own province; and I believe that this superiority of intelligence is due to the fact that our people use a lot of fish. I do not wish to depreciate the food products of other parts of the Dominion, but I certainly think that this valuable food produced in the Maritime provinces should be used more extensively in Canada; and although I have nothing whatever but admiration for the good qualities of the women of

the West, I do not think that they are quite as skilled in the art of cooking fish as are the ladies of the Maritime provinces. It does not matter what hotel you visit in the Maritime provinces, you will find the fish excellent and well cooked. If the art of cooking fish were more extensively practised throughout this country, more fish would be used. To be serious I would impress upon the minister and the committee this fact: The fishermen of the Maritime provinces are becoming disheartened and are leaving the country for the United States. Family after family have gone and we are losing many of the pioneers of this country. So far as the Maritime provinces are concerned, we are losing the flower of our population. The fishing industry is one of the oldest of our activities -in this country. I was astonished on entering the legislature of the state of Massachusetts some time ago to see in front of the speaker's chair, as the emblem of the state, a golden codfish. But so far as my knowledge of the Canadian parliament goes, and judging from the reports 1 have read of the proceedings in this House during the past twenty years, if a man stood up and ventured to talk about fish he was regarded as a faddist. Briefly, these are the facts' About 1909 a non-incorporated association was formed at Margaree in the county of Inverness for the purpose of supplying parent salmon to the government hatchery which was established in that vicinity about that time. The association originally consisted of a relatively small number of members, but in 1910 the membership was brought up to nineteen and continued at this figure until the summer of 1922. Several of the original members died in the meantime and their places were filled by their widows or elder sons, by agreement in every case.
The association, subject to the direction of the superintendent of the pond, so called,- an official of the Department of Marine and Fisheries-laid the fish trap each year, at the expense of its members; that is to say, the trap was the property of the members of the association, and while they were an unincorporated body, yet there was a contractual relation existing between the members and the department to supply these parent fish. In every case the material has been paid for by members of the association. At the annual meeting of 1922 the year's business was provided for as usual, and a contract was made with one of the members for setting a trap and no question of additional membership was raised. On the 4th of August, 1922, the president of the association, Mr. Severin Arsenault, got orders from the department by wire to have the trap set. At the same time he states he got orders from the hon. member for Inverness in this house (Mr. Chisholm) to exclude from the list of persons to be served with notice to set the trap, the names of five Conservatives and to include five Liberals in their places. Arsenault carried out his instructions, but the Conservatives nevertheless turned up and did their part in the work.
About the same time, namely on August 9th, J. A. Rodd, Superintendent of Fish Culture of the Fisheries branch of the department, wrote to P. D. LeBlanc, superintendent *of the pond at Margaree, stating that the department "understands that the present membership of the association is as follows" and {Mr. Hanson.]
proceeded to eliminate the five Conservatives and include the five new Liberals. On learning the names included in this list John C. LeBlanc-one of the Conservatives-wrote to Mr. Rodd protesting and explaining what the situation really was. Mr. Rodd replied on August 31st disclaiming any intention of determining the question of membership but proceeded as follows: "The information before the department showed that the membership for the present year consisted of the persons whose names were communicated to the Superintendent of the Pond"-referring of course to the letter of August 4th to P. D. LeBlanc. J. C. LeBlanc replied to this at length on September 13th pressing for the sources from which the department obtained its "information." The department replied on September 20th in the usual vein, not disclosing its source of information.
On December 18th the secretary-treasurer of the association, Thos. J. LeBlanc, also one of the Conservatives, wrote to the department asking for the cheque in payment of the association's account for the year. In previous years the cheque had, properly, been sent to the secretary-treasurer. He waited a month for a reply which, under date of January 17, 1923, informed him that "a cheque has been issued and forwarded to Severin Arsen

suit the president for distribution amongst those who are entitled to any portion of it."

I am much obliged to
my hon. friend (Mr. Hanson) for bringing this matter up. It has been a subject that he has evidently taken a great deal of interest in.
First let me tell him for his information that when he talks about the politics of these men he does not know the first thing about it. There were Liberals and Tories in what he calls the association. There were Liberals and Tories who ceased to be members of that so-called organization, and let me remind him that some of these men that he seems to stand up for to-night were supporters of mine and not supporters of the Tory party.
Let me tell you, Mr. Chairman, the history of this matter. If my hon. friend had just taken the trouble of discussing it with me, as I would have done with him, were the circumstances reversed, he would have been in a much better position to discuss this question intelligently. He evidently does not know the first thing about it.
Some years ago the department in their wisdom thought fit to pass a regulation preventing the setting of salmon nets in the tidal waters of the rivers of Canada, including the Margaree river. At that time there were several people, perhaps twenty-five, setting nets in the Margaree river. They were getting a little revenue from it. When the regulation was passed, the department of course prevented them from setting their nets. About this time a fish pond was opened up there for salmon to supply the hatchery and I suggested to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that it would be a good thing for him to give the business of catching these salmon for the pond to some of the men who were deprived of the right of putting their nets in the river. At that time I suggested the names of seventeen men. Afterwards the names of two additional men were added, but that did not at all comprise the number of men that used to operate nets in the river previous to this regulation, preventing the setting of nets in the Margaree. These nineteen men were operating-that is were getting these salmon for the fish pond up until last year. I have no compunction in the world in telling my hon. friend, if it will bring any comfort to his soul, that I suggested myself that a

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
change should be made. I will tell him the reason why. I did not think it was right to continue this thing as an apparent favour to a few people while their neighbours were deprived of it-neighbours who were entitled to consideration. I suggested to the department that they drop five of these men and take up five more, and let me tell my hon. friend that most of the people living in that section, yes, 80 per cent of them are supporters of mine. I did this simply from the standpoint of justice and fairness and did not do it without the knowledge of these men-one and all of them. I said I would recommend that five of these men would be dropped and some more of the remaining 17 would be dropped later, until we were able to give each one of the men who were deprived of net fishing in Margaree by government regulations their turn of this somewhat valuable privilege. I propose to follow up that policy. Notwithstanding the moral lecture my hon. friend has been giving me I propose following it up and seeing to it that all the men who enjoy the right of putting nets in the Margaree river will have a turn at this privilege in so far as the trap is concerned. I am not a lawyer and I cannot understand the mentality of my hon. friend when he attaches any guilt to the department whatsoever. The department said to a certain number of men down there "We want you to get salmon for the pond and we will pay you so much." These men got together and they bought a trap. The fact that the trap was bought and paid for is one matter. It was not paid for by the department. The department had nothing at all to do with it. All the department had to do was to tell their agent down there to see that a proper trap was provided, that is, a trap suitable for the purpose, and to see that the salmon were properly looked after until they found their way into the pond. That is all the department had to do with it. Let me tell my good friend something else: When these five men were going to be added in place of the five that were dropped they went to the five that were dropped and told them "We will pay you the value of your part of the trap, we are prepared to do it any time." The seventeen men were in this position. When the time came I made a recommendation to the department.-I say this right now in the presence of my hon. friend and if he can take any comfort out of it or if he can see anything unmoral in that he can view it according to his own judgment-I suggested to the department to put those five men in place of the five to be dropped. These seventeen who were left in
[Mr. Chisholm.1
had a trap on their hands and there was only one of two things for them to do: They would either have to operate this trap or buy a new trap because evidently they could not satisfy the other five men for the reason that they expected to enjoy this privilege in perpetuity, they expected it was to be everlasting. They have discovered, however, that it was not going to be done and I will assure my hon. friend it will not be done. I will tell him something more: As a lawyer he, in my judgment, should refrain from discussing a matter that is before the courts, as he says. This, I tell him, is a primary principle of law as I understand it. In the judgment of the court in Nova Scotia my hon. friend may find himself sadly mistaken, and it may be a salutary lesson to him. Now, as to the cheques. The cheques were sent down by the department with instructions to pay the money to those to whom the money was due and a list of these men was sent to the party to whom the list was sent. To whom else should the money be paid? The day the trap was put into the water the agent of the government there told these five men dropped "You have no right here. My instructions are that these nineteen men are to operate these traps." Here comes in my guilt again because I suggested this change. I thought it proper to make a change in order to pass the privilege over to some other men who were entitled to it. The five men dropped had not the privilege of setting a trap in the river-that privilege could only be given to them by the department, which privilege was actually refused to them by the authorized agent of the department.
Does the hon. gentleman think that it is a matter of good conscience to deprive five owners of their property without compensation, or even to attempt to force them to sell out their interests?

I can tell my hon. friend that I am just as conscientious as he is, and that I have just as much regard for a man's privileges or rights as he has. I told him that when these five new men went in they saw the old men whose places they were taking, as my hon. friend says, and told them "We will pay you for your property." The only property they had was one nineteenth of the value of the traps each.

I have the following memorandum:
The board was established by Act of Parliament (2 George V, chap. 6) in 1912 and has charge of all biological stations in Canada and the conduct and control of marine biological investigations. While the board is, in the main, a volunteer organization, the members and investigators not being paid, it arranges the investigations so as to throw light on matters connected with the life history of fish, their origin, development, structure, functions, distribution, etc., and reasons for deterioration, etc. Permanent biological stations are maintained at St. Andrews, N.S., and at Departure bay, Nanaimo, B.C., and a small sea-going vessel is also maintained on the Atlantic coast. In addition to the permanent stations, seasonal or temporary stations are established from time to time and at various points as occasion requires.

The Chief Inspector of Fisheries has no time to devote to the study of fishery questions. He has no time to devote to the study of hatcheries. He has no time to devote to the study of the habits of fish. This requires some man to be on hand all the time who can devote his fullest attention to studying fishery matters. I suggested at one time to the late minister the necessity for having someone out in British Columbia who could co-operate with the Chief Inspector of Fisheries and who could be ready and available at all times for the purpose of making these scientific investigations. I am glad to hear that the minister is making an arrangement to get another scientific man on his staff in British Columbia. I would suggest to him that it will not be sufficient for him to employ university professors during their vacation, but rather, that the department should have on hand some one or, perhaps, two scientific men of experience who will be available at all times on this important work.

I might also explain this mattei. For the last six or seven years there has been in existence a fleet, valued at some three or four million dollars, pre-war prices, of dredges, scows and tugs on the Richelieu river and the Chenal du Moine. This fleet was in a state of deterioration for want of proper care and attention. I took hold of the department in the month of August, acting for my hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe) who was at Geneva, and I made a personal inspection of the Sorel shipyard and looked over all the ships, dredges and scows that were there. I discovered that one of the dredges had sunk simply from lack of proper care. The rust had corroded the steel and the vessel was down, and when I asked what it would require to salvage this vessel I found that it would cost about 817,000. I took the superintendent of the St. Lawrence channel, together with the foreman of the yards at Sorel, and made a thorough inspection of the boats. I asked them to tell me which of them could be preserved, which ought to be scrapped, and which could be salvaged. Accompanying me was my secretary, and as I say, there were the superintendent of the St. Lawrence channel and the superintendent of the yards.
We went over every ship and found that certain hulls would have to be scrapped, while there was a certain percentage of the machinery that could be salvaged. It was found that a shed would be necessary, and that a quantity of paint would be required to prevent the steel work from deteriorating. For this work it was estimated that the sum of $80,000 would be called for. I came back with a detailed statement covering each ship, scow and dredge, and recommended to council that this fleet, which was worth, as I have stated, some three or four million dollars, should be salvaged as far as possible. Under the circumstances it was considered that the special warrant should be issued. That warrant was issued in order that the work might be proceeded with at once. I did this as a matter of sound business, to prevent the further . deterioration of this valuable fleet, and it resulted in saving money to the country. That is the whole matter in a nutshell.

Is this in consequence of a mistaken idea that at one time prevailed regarding our jurisdiction over False creek? Otherwise, when the Canadian Pacific Railway crossed there why were not the usual terms imposed?

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

The explanation in regard to this was given last year, but I will repeat it. It is as follows:
The Canadian Pacific Railway constructed a bridge across False creek, Vancouver, in 1886. This bridge was replaced by a larger structure in 1898. In 1918 it transpired that the vessels being constructed at the Coughlan Shipyard for the Imperial Munitions Board could not pass to sea without the removal of a span of this bridge. This difficulty was the subject of negotiations between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Department of Public Works at that time. The Canadian Pacific Railway contended that the bridge was properly constructed with the approval of the Public Works department and consequently they were under no obligations to so alter the bridge as to make it possible for vessels of a larger class to pass through. In these circumstances it became necessary for some one to take action, and the undersigned after having discussed the matter fully with the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, entered into negotiations with Mr. Beatty of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the result being the submission of a proposal that if the courts should decide that the bridge was properly constructed and had the approval of the Public Works department, the govermnent would be responsible for the expense of removing the span to enable the vessels being constructed at the Coughlan yards to pass out. On the other hand if the courts should determine that the bridge was improperly constructed and did not have the approval of the Public Works department, the Canadian Pacific Railway would be responsible for any expenditure incurred for the removal of the span. Letters were exchanged between this department and the Canadian Pacific Railway confirming this understanding. In the meantime the matter was referred to the Department of Justice for an opinion and under date of the 20th instant-
That was June of last year.
that department writes as per copy attached hereto.
The Department of Justice stated that we had absolutely no case against the Canadian Pacific Railway.
In these circumstances there does not appear to be any alternative but to ask for a special vote of parliament to indemnify the Canadian Pacific Railway for the expenses they have incurred in this connection. Last session a sum of $32,000 was placed in Supplementary Estimates 1922-23 to cover expenditure up to end of June 1920, but a statement of expenditure up to 31st October, 1921, shows that the total expenditure incurred in this connection is $40,934.08, necessitating a further amount of $8,934.08.

Negotiations are being conducted between the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Marine and Fisheries and Public Works departments to come to a final arrangement in the matter.

That is the purpose in view.

Canada and the West Indies and South America, or both, steam service or services between, $340,666.66.
Could the minister give us the names of the boats engaged in this subsidized service, with the tonnage and passenger capacity of each?

The boats are the Chignecto, 400 feet; the Chaleur, 400 feet; the Caraquet, 400 feet, and the Chaudiere, 370 feet. Three of these vessels were built in Belfast, and one in Middlesborough, one in 1S93, one in 1S94, and one in 1899. I might say to my hon. friend that these boats are a bit old and a little slow, and we are advertising for a new service extending over two different periods. We are asking for tenders for a five-year period and also for a ten-year period, and when the tenders are in the government will decide which will be most advantageous to Canada. As perhaps my hon. friend knows, this is part of the contract we have with the West India islands under the trade agreement made in 1920.

The minister has not given the information I asked for. 1 did not ask for the length of the boats. I wanted their tonnage and passenger capacity. I should also like to know their 3peed. I want to find out whether they comply with the terms of the West India agreement.

I may say frankly that we fear they do not, and that is why we are asking for new tenders. Under the contract we had a certain limit of time within which to provide for the ships, and we are now advertising for four new ships to give a fortnightly service. Perhaps this admission that we do not think these boats comply with the terms of the contract for the West India service will satisfy my hon. friend.

I am quite satisfied they do not comply with the terms either as regards tonnage, speed or passenger capacity. I would ask the minister whether there are not any ships of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine that would comply equally well with the requirements of the West India trade.

No. They are very far from complying with the requirements. There are two services, one on the west side, and another on the east side. The Royal Mail Line are the contractors on the eastern side, and the Canadian Government Merchant Marine have the service on the west side, but they are

Supply-Trade and Commerce
very far from complying with the requirements of the trade, and our friends in the West India islands are objecting somewhat on that account. The previous government advertised for tenders, and my recollection is that they came in either just before this government assumed office or immediately afterwards. The-terms were such that the government did not feel able to accept them. The tenderers asked for a guarantee of 7 per cent upon their investment. We did not think that would be profitable to this country. We preferred knowing exactly what we would have to pay rather than give a guarantee on the investment.
May I ask whether the Canadian Government Merchant Marine vessels are operating in competition with the other vessels of which the minister spoke?

The Royal Mail Line have complained that the Government Merchant Marine boats call at some ports and pick up some of the best cargoes, but we do not admit that. They are not operating in competition with the Royal Mail Line because as I mentioned a moment ago there are two services, one on the east and one on the west side. The trade agreement of 1920 calls for two distinct services, and the Royal Mail Line are running from St. John and Halifax to Barbados, Trinidad, Bermuda, the Leeward islands and the Windward islands. The merchant marine boats run to the Bahamas. Jamaica and British Honduras, so there is really no competition between the two, although the Royal Mail Line have complained that in some cases the government boats on the return trip pick up some very profitable cargoes. We do not admit that that is a disadvantage to the people of Canada. It is competition that means cheaper products for our people.

Under the agreement it was provided that the service was to be weekly. The minister has just stated that tenders are being called for for a fortnightly service. How does he expect, therefore, that these new steamers sailing fortnightly will comply with the terms of the West Indies agreement?

The experience we have is that a fortnightly service will be all that the trade will warrant. I do not believe that Canada can pay for a weekly service in view of the business that offers down in those islands.

Does the minister mean to cut the estimate one-half in view of the fact that we only get one-half the service?

Mr. R)3BB: We cannot disclose what the policy of the department will be until we receive tenders.

Yes.

If the
minister can give the information I am willing to go on.

I have here this memorandum on the western group which may help my hon. friend on the question. Article 15 reads as follows:
Article XV. The government of Canada, subject to the adoption by the governments concerned of the recommendations embodied in Article XVI, undertakes to provide as soon as possible, and in any case not later than 'the 1st January, 1921, a fortnightly freight, mail and passenger steamship service between Canada, the Bahamas, Jamaica, and British Honduras, on the following lines:
The Canadian Government Merchant Marine, therefore, at the request of the Dominion government, took two of their smaller ships and converted them into passenger and freight vessels, by the addition of cabin accommodation, and put them on this route. It was impossible, however, to provide a fortnightly service, as called for by the agreement, with only two ships. These ships have therefore been sailing every three weeks, from Montreal in the summer, and Halifax in winter. The loss on their operation -I ask my hon. friends to note this-has been heavy, amounting, in the year 1921, to over $400,000, or more than the total subsidy paid by the government to the four steamers of the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company, which performed a more frequent and extensive service with more suitably fitted boats than the two steamers of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.
Since that time has the Canadian Government Merchant Marine put on some larger boats?
We have tried to improve the service.

I should like to ask about this treaty, because I really must confess ignorance. The minister stated a little while ago that under the terms of the treaty there had to be a weekly service. Now he states it is only fortnightly. Are the terms of the treaty in this respect elastic or what is the actual -condition?
My hon. friend can obtain a copy of the treaty. It is printed and quite lengthy.
What treaty is that?
The treaty of 1920.
With Jamaica?

Yes. It is somewhat elastic. It was an agreement made for ten years. The
government of Canada have every desire to meet our West India friends. We want that trade for Canada if we can secure it, but we do not want to pay out more for the service than the business will warrant.
Are there any ships of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine that can perform this service at the present time?
This particular service is now being performed by the vessels of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine and by no others.
But not the whole service, just one service?

The service to Jamaica, Bahamas and British Honduras is being performed by the ships of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. The other service, to Bermuda, Trinidad, and British Guiana is being performed under contract by the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company?

I understand that. 1 have here the report of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine and it gives particulars of the service to the West Indies. I notice that Sir Henry Thornton in his report claims there has not been freight enough. He says:
The combined passenger and freight steamship operation inaugurated to give service every three weeks to the Bahamas, Jamaica and British Honduras, from the outset, has been unprofitable from a revenue standpoint, and in an endeavour to reduce losses Bermuda was added to the itinerary in June, the Canadian Fisher and the Canadian Forester making Hamilton, Bermuda, an additional port of call.
It looks to me as though all this service could be performed by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. I would like to read for the information of the House the resolution passed by the district council of the province of Quebec, comprising councils No. 5, 8, 9 and 17 of the National Association of Marine in Canada. In part the resolution reads as follows:
Whereas, subsidies have been granted to steamship companies owned and operated outside Canada, particularly to the West Indies, while Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships, owned by the people of Canada, are lying idle and our seamen walking the streets of our towns and cities, swelling the unemployed. Under the West Indies-Canada agreement the Canadian government was to furnish the ships for this West Indies and British Honduras freight and passenger service:
It seems to me to be extraordinary to pay out a very large amount of money in subsidizing other ships while the vessels of our own merchant marine are lying idle. I have a

letter here from a seafaring man, a former officer in the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, and he states that there are ships of 3,400 tons of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine that can very well be utilized on this route. This matter
was discussed a year ago when the same estimate was being considered, and the same criticism was offered by some hon. gentlemen that is being offered to-night.

There was
very considerable criticism last year, I have not heard much to-night. The suggestion is made that this service could be carried on by the vessels of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. The larger service is that from the Atlantic ports of Halifax and St. John to Bermuda, Trinidad, Demerara, and British Guiana. That service is being carried on by a company known as the Royal Mail Steam Packet company. I think that is the name of the company.

I think it is
the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company. Possibly I may have omitted a word from the title but I do not think my hon. friend would mind that particularly because that would not affect the question. I hope he does not think so, I hope his mind is centered on something more substantial. This contract was entered into some ten or fifteen years ago. At that time a trade treaty was entered into between Canada, certain of the British West India Islands, and the government of Great Britain, and a part of that treaty was that a freight and passenger service be installed or established and subsi-

dized by the interested parties. I think the British government pays something on account of that service as well.

Does the
hon. member say that the British government pays part of the subsidy?

I think they
do, on account of the mail service.

The hon.
member is not sure.

I am not too sure. I speak subject to correction. In order to obtain the service-and it was deemed to be important-it was necessary to subsidize it. No private capital would go and perform such a service voluntarily and carry the mail without a subsidy. Persons who are acquainted with the West Indian trade know that the freight bound for Canadian ports is available only at certain seasons; that is, in the crop moving season, when the sugar, coffee and cocoa crops are being moved. But for two or three months in the year the steamers go north with very little freight. Then a very important consideration for those requiring the service was that it should be a regular service, and that was its great value-that every two weeks a ship would leave an Atlantic port for a West Indian port. That is of inestimable value to exporters. If they did not know or were not sure that these steamships left with perfect regularity we could never have developed the trade we have with the British West Indies. The Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships could not perform that service. They were never built for it, in the first place. Some of these ships run very irregularly to some of the islands, taking their chances of getting a cargo north and south. I have seen some of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships advertised to leave Halifax on a certain day, and they would not leave for nearly a month after, waiting for freight. It is an essential factor in the development of trade to have a regular transportation system, so that the importer and exporter can rely upon the regularity and promptness of that service. The Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships were not built for such a service. They were not built to carry on a passenger service at all, and we would have to violate the treaty which was entered into with the West Indian islands if we abandoned the service altogether, and declined to carry on the present contract, or a new contract with some other shipping concern. It certainly could not be carried on by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships because they cannot
