but you will realize that there may be a partial compliance with the agreement by the merchant marine, but there can only be a partial compliance.

The Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships could not carry on the service at all, wholly or partially or fractionally. It may be true that the Royal Mail boats are not performing the service well within the obligations of that treaty. I am not sure about that. My own impression is that they are, but everybody realizes that the ships they have now in the service are old and inadequate, and the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company themselves have publicly made clear their realization of that fact, and their desire to construct four new steamers, more modern boats, and put them into that service. It is for that reason they would like to have a long term contract with the government and boats specially designed for that sendee. The boats now in the service were quite old when the treaty was entered into. Nobody, I am sure, realizes more than that company itself that the boats are hardly up to the requirements of the trade, although they may be well within the requirements of the treaty. Now trade has developed and travel has developed, and it is desirable that
a better service be given between Canadian ports and the West Indies, and we can never get the service without paying some subsidy. We cannot, I think, continue our thide arrangements with the British West Indies unless we assist that service. We certainly cannot give a regular mail service, which is a very important factor in trade, unless we have boats sailing promptly and ar, regular intervals from Canadian and West Indian ports.
Has the hon. member any idea of the amount of trade that is done on this line as far as Canada is concerned?

I have not
seen the figures lately. Usually I have these figures in my mind and am well acquainted with them, but I do not know them at the present moment. The trade has been very irregular and rather depressed in recent years. I fancy it has been unprofitable to the steamship company. I think during the war they probably lost a very considerable sum; at least they would have, had they not been permitted to raise their rates, but I want to assure my hon. friend, if he thinks our trade connection with the British West Indies is worth anything to this country-and it is-that it can only be kept up by the continuance of this service. Now the Canadian Government Merchant Marine have some boats running to these islands that are served by the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company. I think myself it is very foolish to have these ships competing with the steamship line which is subsidized, and I do not think they contribute anything to the development of our trade.
Just a word as to the service between Canada, Jamaica and British Honduras. I have not any personal knowledge of this service, except that I have a little knowledge that comes to me from those who are interested in trading between Nova Scotia and these islands. This treaty was entered into in 1920, I think at a time when Canalians and people generally gained a clear vizualization of the future trade not only between Canada and these islands, but the world over, and I fear that rather an extravagant bargain was made in the establishment of this service. It does not appear that there is a possibility of developing a trade that would warrant the cost to this country last year. I am informed by business men who know, whose firms have been trading with those islands for the last fifty, seventy-five or a hundred years, that it is not possible to develop trade with those islands to warrant the service that is being carried on at the present time. I have no particular

3382	' COMMONS
Supply-Trade and Commerce
suggestion to make to the minister about the matter, except that it requires careful consideration. It would be far better to give to some private companies two or three of these Canadian government ships and let them operate the service in the best possible way. It need not be a regular passenger service. I think the passenger service should be cut out altogether. The boats are not suitable for the service and this is costing money. We are carrying passengers, mostly tourists, over this route at a great loss to the country. There would be better satisfaction, and I believe the people of the islands interested would be satisfied if a fair freight service might be given to them, and I think that is possible at a very much less cost than that at which the service is being carried on to-day.

The hon.
gentleman is speaking of the western group just now, is he not?
Jamaica, the Bahamas and British Honduras.
That would be the western group.
Yes.
The Canadian Government Merchant Marine.
It is operating there.
The hon. member thinks the service should be cut off?

I do not say that it should be cut off; but I understand that it was carried on last year at a net loss of $400,000, and I am informed by persons who know the possibilities of trade in those islands, that it is not capable of any great expansion.
Does the same statement not apply to the eastern group that it is unprofitable business at the present time? Why do they want a subsidy if the business pays?
No subsidy is being paid.
I am talking about the eastern group now.

No subsidy is being paid by the other group. Our trade has developed with the British West Indies, but our trading with those islands is linked up with the subsidized steamship service.

You cannot separate them. We have a trade prefemce with these islands, and one of the conditions of the preference was that this steamship which is a joint passenger, freight and mail service, should be carried on. You cannot drop one without dropping the other. They are linked together.

The preference is an expensive one.
Mr. .MACLEAN (Halifax): I doubt if any shipping company would undertake to carry on the service without a subsidy.
For what length of time will that treaty run?
For ten years.
From what date?

From 1920. I have the information for which my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Shaw) asked as to the trade with those islands. I am speaking now of the British West Indies, and I will not give the figures exactly. In 1922, the total trade was $15,300,000 and in 1923, $18,500,000. I am sure my hon. friends will realize that it is worth something to Canada to have this good customer. We expect, as the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has said, that with improved facilities this trade may grow. Perhaps I might put on Hansard, although this will take a little time, the advertisement for tenders, and let me say at this point that if the Canadian Government Merchant Marine or Sir Henry Thornton desires to tender for this service and can give the service and comply with the conditions, surely we will give the preference to our own vessels.
He cannot tender.
I am not questioning whether he can tender or not.
He cannot tender.

This is the advertisement for tenders:
1.	Tenders for a mail, passenger and freight steamship service between Canada, the British West Indies and British Guiana, are invited, and will be received at the office of the Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce, Ottawa, Canada, until noon of June 15, 1923.
2.	Tenders must be submitted on the enclosed form, and should be sent in sealed envelopes, addressed to the Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce, Ottawa, Canada, and marked legibly on the outside "Tenders for steamship service between Canada, the British West Indies and British Guiana", and if submitted through the mails should be registered.
3.	Tenders are invited for the performance of one or more of the following services:

Supply-Trade and Commerce
(a)	Sailing fortnightly from St. John or Halifax, and calling one week on the outward passage at Bermuda, Barbados, Trinidad, and British Guiana, and on the homeward passage at Trinidad, Grenada, St. Vincent, Barbados, St. Lucia, Dominica, Montserrat, Antigua, Nevis, St. Kitts, and Bermuda; and on alternate weeks calling on the outward passage at Bermuda, St. Kitts, Nevil, Antigua, Montserrat, Dominica, St. Lucia, Barbados, St. Vincent, Grenada, Trinidad, and British Guiana, and on the homeward passage at Trinidad, Barbados and Bermuda.
(b)	The same service as specified in Clause (a) except that sailings shall be made from St. John and Halifax alternately.
(c)	Any other frequency of service, or itinerary, or other variation from the terms of this call for tenders, which tenderers may desire to offer.
4.	Tenders are invited for service covering a period of five or ten years, commencing within two weeks after the date of the last sailing from Halifax under the present contract which expires on March 31, 1924.
5.	The steamers to be employed should be from 5,000 to 6,000 tons gross, capable of maintaining an ocean speed of 12 knots, and providing accommodation for 100 first class, 30 second class, and 100 steerage or deck passengers, and should be provided with 'tween decks.
6.	The tender must state the amount of subsidy required, and the period for which the contract is requested.
7.	The contract will ^provide that there shall be reasonable proportionate allocation of passengers and cargo accommodation between the colonies mentioned in Clause 3 (a).
8.	There shall be no unfair differentiation in rates of freight against the smaller colonies as compared with the rates of larger colonies situated at a similar distance from St. John or Halifax, and freight and passenger rates will at all times be subject to the approval of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
9.	The steamers should be so constructed that, so far as the traffic warrants, cold storage shall be provided, but alternative tenders may be submitted offering the steamers with or without cold storage.
10.	The steamers employed shall at all times, if required, carry such mails as may be offered for that purpose by the postal authorities of Canada, or the West Indian Colonies, and the contractor is to land and embark all mails at terminal points and ports of call at his own expense.
11.	The contract will be subject to such general conditions as are incidental to all similar steamship subsidy contracts granted by the Canadian government.
12.	Any further information required in regard to this call for tenders may be obtained on application to the undersigned.
13.	The minister does not bind himself to accept the lowest or any tender.
The committee will observe that there is an option of five or ten years. These tenders are due, I think, on the fifteenth June of this year, and after the tenders are in and the government have had time to consider them, they are at liberty to accept or reject any of the tenders.

The minister, I think, has given the committee the impression that the subsidy is justifiable because of the fact that a trade treaty has been 216i
entered into, and under it a certain steamship service is required. Is that the case?

That was part of the treaty; but we had a subsidy there before the treaty because it is worth something to the Dominion of Canada to have a customer with whom we do a bus-ness amounting to $18,000,000 a year. There is no railway communication down to those islands, and you cannot get the business except by a steamship service. We have a considerable preference in that market for our products, and we ship to those islands large quantities of flour. The Dominion of Canada practically controls the trade in flou-of the West Indian islands, because we hav-1 a considerable preference on flour. We also ship to those islands large quantities of dairy products and fish. It is largely agricultural products that are shipped down there, and in return they send us back products which we require in this country, such as fruit which we cannot grow here, and sugar. I submit that it is a fair trade between Canada and the West Indian islands.

I had not quite finished my question. I presumed, however, it was because of the treaty and the requirement of the regular sailings that the subsidy was being continued. The tender that has just been read calls for a fortnightly service, but the treaty calls for a weekly service. Even if you get the new and improved boats with the new subsidy under the new tender, you still do not comply with the trade agreement.
Which treaty was that-the first or the second?
The last treat3r, the one that is now effective.

My hon. friend must understand that there are two parties to a bargain. The people who are doing the business down there intimate that it will not pay. I will put on record the memorandum I have as regards the whole business down there:
Under the agreement, the Canadian government, pledged itself to "use its best endeavours"-
That was the pledge.
-to arrange for a mail, passenger and freight service, to come into effect as soon as possible, and in any case within three years, between Canada and the eastern group (see article X).t
In order to carry out this part of the agreement, th 'refore, the government called for tenders for this service on September 20, 1921, receivable up to noon of January 31, 1922. When the last mentioned time arrived, only one tender had been received, and this was from the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company, the

Supply-Trade and Commerce
present contractors. The Canada West Indies Trade agreement contemplates the establishment of a weekly service. The Royal Mail Steam Packet Co., however, pointed out that there is not sufficient trade on this route to keep up a weekly service, and that any attempt to run such a service would be followed by a heavy loss. They, therefore, propose to put on a fortnightly service. As it would be necessary to build four new ships for this route they wanted a contract for the life of such ships, viz. twenty years, They stated that they could not afford to run the proposed new service for a fixed subsidy while the steamers of the C.G.M.M. were at the same time running in competition with subsidized vessels. The R.M.S.P. had previous to this been making complaints to the effect that the C.G.M.M. ships came into Trinidad, Barbados and Demerara, and took away a large proportion of their most profitable cargo,-
That is, on the homeward voyage. There is not enough business for both services on the homeward voyage, although there is quite enough for both going down. It is in the interests of the Canadian people for us to send all the business we can down there.

But if they are to take
freight down they must bring freight back.

-that is, sugar and molasses. The Royal Mail Steam Packet Company protested against this, stating that while it is admitted that there is sufficient southbound traffic for both lines, yet the northbound cargo is limited in quantity and there is not sufficient for both lines.
I would emphasize the fact that there is a good deal of business going down, but (he complaint is that our vessels take away from their freight coming back. I am not debating the question whether they are right or wrong, but that is their complaint.
The R.M.S.P. offered, therefore, to provide a fortnightly service with new steamers of the size and type contemplated by the West Indies Agreement, on condition that the government guaranteed a minimum return of 7$ per cent per annum on the capital value of the said new ships. It may be added here that the present revenue on this service works out at between three and five per cent on the capital value of the four old steamers which the R.M.S.P. are running, after taking the subsidy into account.
We did not accept that contract. We are how submitting tenders which will be opened in June and the government are using their best endeavours to meet the desire of the West India islands because we want to keep those customers of ours, provided, of course, that the service is not too expensive.

Do I understand that the
stipulations of the advertisement just read do not comply with the terms of the treaty? If so, what would be the use of securing a contract of that kind? What is the penalty in the event of the treaty being violated?

Our friends in the West Indies (ire not unreasonable, and I do not think that

they are prepared to pay their proportion of the cost if the traffic does not warrant a weekly service. Now, I do not know on whose behalf hon. gentlemen are complaining. We have had a communication with the people there, and I have here a message the Prime Minister transmitted.

I am not complaining at all.
I confess at once that I know very little about this matter, but it struck me that it might be idle to call for tenders if the service would not comply with the treaty; I thought we might not get the benefit of it. I should think it would be essential to make sure that the other parties to the treaty would be satisfied with the stipulations in the tender. One would suppose that this would be a condition precedent to the acceptance of any tender. Is it the intention of the department, even if the tenders are thought satisfactory, to accept them without making certain of the satisfaction of the other parties to the treaty? If they were not satisfied, it might involve a variation in the terms of the treaty.

We will certainly not enter
into a contract unless it is acceptable to the West Indies.

I suggest
that it is hardly fair for the minister to characterize as complaints a very fair criticism of a very questionable looking item.
It is not questionable.

There are one or
two points that are not clear, if this is to be anything like an intelligent presentation of the case. According to the very statement just now read by the minister, the Canadian Government Marine is in competition with a subsidized line.
That is the complaint.

That is the complaint, and I presume it has some foundation. If that is so, then it is the very point that leads some of us to object to the item. I confess that it does seem very strange, to me at least, that there should be a large subsidy like this granted by the government to a steamship line when at the same time we have our own Canadian Government Merchant Marine vessels in competition with that line. I do not wonder that our vessels are losing, where they are in competition with a line subsidized against us by ourselves. That is the main point, and I do not think it has yet been answered. The statement has been made by the minister, I think, and by

Supply-Trade and Commerce
the member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) that the Canadian Marine boats are not suitable for this route. Are there any boats belonging to the government that can be made suitable for it?
No.

I do not know
anything about shipping on the east coast, although I do know something about the conditions on the west coast. But I was talking with a captain of one of the Canadian Government boats a few months ago and he informed me that some of these vessels could very readily be converted to meet the needs of that route. He must know what he is talking about because he is on that run himself. He said that very few additions would be necessary to provide a passenger service, and that if there were cold storage facilities these boats could bring back a very profitable return cargo in the form of fruit, and so forth, coming to Canada. Has there been any thorough-going investigation of the possibilities of this route, or has there been any authoritative report on the subject?

I know nothing about steamships myself and I do not pretend to know anything about them. But if the gentlemen who are responsible to the Dominion of Canada for the management of the Government Merchant Marine, and who undoubtedly should know a great deal about vessels, consider that any of the government boats can be so equipped as to meet the requirements of the route without involving too great an expense, I have no doubt they will so inform the government. As I have pointed out, we are asking for tenders.

Have we had any
report on the subject?

Tenders will be opened, on
June 15th. I might repeat that there is no complaint as regards the service going down; there is ample business on the downward trip. The complaint has reference to the upward voyage; they claim that we take away business from the subsidized line. We must remember that while the Canadian Government Marine has made a loss, the people of Canada have had some -advantage from the reduced freight.
My information is that last season the Royal Mail Steamship Company raised its rates 25 per cent.
We have no complaint on record.
The department would have to consent to the increase?
We have no complaint of the rates.

The remarks of the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) are quite natural. It is only fair to concede the fact that persons not acquainted -with this particular trade should think it strange that we should be paying $350,000 a year for a steamship service while at the same time we have our own government ships operating in these waters. I am not objecting either to the criticism that the policy of subsidizing steamships is in itself wrong. I must confess that I am not very much enamoured of it. However, in this particular case the steamship service is part of a trade convention. We receive preferential treatment in the West India islands on certain conditions, one of them being the maintenance of this service. I do not know whether some of the vessels of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine might not be made suitable for this service, but their conversion would cost millions of dollars. Personally I have no faith in the government operation of ships. I say it is much cheaper and more satisfactory in every respect to pay a subsidy to a privately-owned line than to have the vessels owned and operated by the government, because such operation [DOT] will always be more expensive. The public will not allow these ships to be operated as carefully and economically as is the case with privately-owned ships. I think therefore that on the whole it is in the interests of the development of Canadian trade to subsidize this private service rather than attempt the conversion of our government vessels at a cost of millions of dollars and then operate them at a cost far in excess, I am sure, of the cost of operation of privately-owned ships.

With respect to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, I made the statement on the floor of this House last session that any ship under five thousand tons would never pay operating expenses. There are some twenty-two of these ships under that tonnage. I repeat that statement to-night, and I do so after going over their plans and specifications very carefully. The sooner the government realizes that these ships cannot possibly be made to pay and gets rid of them the better it will be for the taxpayers. A good deal has been said, possibly not in this House, about the late government building those ships. I am not finding fault with that policy, although I did not approve of it at
33SG

Supply-Trade and Commerce
the time, but they were constructed when most people expected shipping would be good for many years to come. Construction took place at a time when wages and building material were at the very top notch. Last year I went into this question very carefully with the late Mr. Kennedy, then Minister of Railways. In fact he asked me to form a company on the Pacific coast to see if we could not operate these ships, but this I refused to do, because I knew they could not be operated at a profit the way their boilers are constructed. I am not going into this in detail, indeed, it would not be in the interests of the people that I should, because I think it will be better for the country that these ships be disposed of and what I might bring out would not add to the chances of the government getting rid of them. If the government can get 20 per cent of the cost of these ships I think they will be getting a good price; and I question whether they will be able to get even that. If you attempt to convert them into passenger ships they will be a still greater burden, because they have not the required power or speed, and we shall only be getting further into debt for something that will never be a paying proposition.
As it is twelve o'clock and this is a very important item I would ask that it be allowed to stand over.
We have been spending hours on this item, and surely we ought to get it through now.
Then we will spend more hours on it, Mr. Chairman.

speechtext:
Shall the resolution
carry?
Will the minister tell us the profits of the Royal Mail Steam Packet Line for last year?
I think I gave that a few moments ago. I have not the information under my hand just now, but it was about 5 per cent on the investment. It will be found on Hansard.
It may be on Hansard, but I should like to get it now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister is not required to give information twice on the same vote.
I am not sure that he even gave it once.
Yes, I gave the information.

The minister simply said he thought it was 5 per cent. I think we are entitled to know the exact amount in dollars of the profit or loss, if any, made by the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company last year.

Sir Henry Thornton
speaks rather optimistically of the prospects for trade in the West Indies, and I am not entirely convinced that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine cannot handle the business.
He will probably tender for the contract.

I have received several pamphlets and letters from practical seamen, one a former officer in the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, and I am assured by them that these vessels could be used to advantage in this trade. I notice in the Official Journal of the Marine Engineers of Canada, published in St. John, New Brunswick, that a Halifax correspondent writes, in part, as follows:
We also have to regret that quite a number of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine are still laid up in the Northwest Arm. These if put in commission would give employment to between 250 and 300 men. I was surprised to read a few days ago that the government had made a new contract for two years with the R.M.S.P. Company to supply the West Indies an d Demerara service. Why could not four of the Canadian Government Merchant fleet be fitted for this work, and thus give employment to our own men and put the charter money into the government coffers? We sincerely trust that the new government will remedy these abuses and bring about a better state of affairs.
Now. notwithstanding all that has been said in criticism of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine I note that it made a small profit in both 1919 and 1920.
On the Pacific.

We must remember, of course, that very few steamship companies have made money of late years. Sir Henry Thornton in his report says:
The steamers, Canadian Fisher and Canadian Forester, in operation on this route, are not suitable for this trade, and it is considered essential, in order to make a success of this branch of the service, that a special type of oil-burning steamers, with increased passenger accommodation, and fitted with proper refrigeration and ventilation facilities to take care of perishable shipments, be provided.
I understand that their specifications come pretty well up to the standard of the other vessels they are competing with, and it does seem to me unreasonable that this amount should be paid out to subsidize vessels operat-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
ing in competition with the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. If the capital investment in the Merchant Marine is too large, it should be written down the same as the American government did with their fleet. They wrote it down I think to about fhty per cent of the capitalization.

The Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships would
have to be reconstructed anyway. The operators would have to come to parliament and ask it to vote the money. Parliament would have to grant it to them, and it has not done so yet.

I quite understand that, but I think this matter should be taken into consideration before any subsidy is granted. Let the government make definite inquiries from the Railway Board as to what can be done and ascertain what the recommendations are. It seems an extraordinary thing to tie the country up for five or ten years to a subsidized service without knowing what our own ships can do. In this same report on the Merchant Marine, Sir Henry Thornton also draws attention to the fact that these ships, while perhaps not paying as a separate branch, are drawing a large amount of freight and bringing tonnage for the Canadian National railways. That also should be taken into consideration.

At this late hour I do not' want to enter into any lengthy discussion. I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) in what he read from Sir Henry Thornton's report has upset his own argument. First he read something from a marine paper which deprecated the fact that some of the Government Merchant Marine steamers in the Northwest arm were out of commission, when they might be giving employment to a certain number of men. Then it went on to say that if they were put in commission they could be used on the West India service. Then my hon. friend read from Sir Henry Thornton's report that the present steamers on the route were not fitted for the business, and that the type of steamer required was an oil burner. That just fixed the hon. gentleman's argument. Sir Henry Thornton admits that there are no steamers in the Government Merchant Marine fitted for this West India service, which includes carrying passengers, mail and freight, and that is an absolute fact. We may talk till we are black and blue, and I do not want to take up time to-night because I shall discuss this matter on another occasion, when I shall be able to prove that there is not one steamer of the
whole sixty-three in the govemmenet fleet that is fitted for carrying passengers, mail and freight. At the present time they are using two or three of these steamers on the Honduras route, and they are carrying practically no freight. At some ports at which they call, at Belize and Jamaica they are landing only five pounds of freight, and these steamers are being run at an expense of three or four thousand dollars a day. My hon. friend is correct about freights being increased, but it was not twenty-five per cent. About two years ago they were increased fifty per cent, and for this reason:	The government
steamers which are competing with the Royal Mail Packet boats on the same route were getting part of the business which the Royal Mail boats should have had if they were to pay, and when the Royal Mail Company found that the Canadian government boats were taking part of the business, which was not sufficient for them both- both lines were carrying only half cargoes- the manager of the Royal Mail Packet came to Ottawa and placed his statement before the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He showed him that they were losing a large sum of money and the Minister of Trade and Commerce called in Mr. Teakle, the manager of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, and asked him what he thought about it. Mr. Teakle said: "Yes, we are not making any money, and instead of getting $2.40 for a cask of fish and $1.10 for a barrel of flour we should get more." The Minister of Trade and Commerce consequently increased the freight rates both on the Canadian Government Merchant Marine and the Royal Mail Packet line. That is exactly what happened.
The trade agreement with the West India islands calls for a twelve-knot service. The Canadian Government Merchant Marine boats cannot comply with that because their speed is only between eight and nine knots, and inside of two years, although as the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) says, we do not want to say too much about it, owing to poor construction these government boats will need new boilers and engines, as their engines and boilers are practically no good.
Would the hon. member tell us if the beats that are now being subsidized are all speedy enough to meet the requirements of that trade?

Yes, I think they are twelve-knot boats. I am a shipper in Nova Scotia and am using these boats, not every fortnight, but every once in awhile, and we are quite
33SS

Supply-Trade and Commerce
satisfied with these boats so far as trade with the West Indies is concerned, although, of course, a faster boat would be better.
You are not sure they are up to the standard.
The Royal Mail Packet boats, yes.
I have here a list of the Royal Mail Packet boats on this service and only one of them is a twelve-knot boat. The others were all built thirty years ago, so they are not very modem.
The contract calls for a twelve-knot service, and I say that the Merchant Marine boats cannot give that service.

Neither could the other
boats.
The minister has not to accept the tender of the Royal Mail Company. He can accept anybody's tender that is satisfactory, yours or mine.

If the Royal Mail Company get the new contract they will have to put on new ships. Their ships were able to comply with the terms of the original contract ten or fifteen years ago, but nobody disputes the fact that these ships now are hardly suitable for the purpose. If they are the successful tenderers these boats will be withdrawn and new boats put on in time.
Why were they not withdrawn last year?

We could not get anyone else to take the service. Let me repeat what I said before. The previous government in September, before going out of office, advertised for tenders. Those tenders came in in January, 1922. The tenderers wanted a guarantee of 7 per cent on their investment, and the government did not consider that that was a profitable bargain for the Dominion, so the best thing we could do was arrange with our West India customers to accept a continuation of the previous service by the Royal Mail Line, and we arranged with them to continue the service. My hon. friend asked a moment ago as to the earnings of this company. I have a notation here that the present revenue-I do not know whether this is profit; we have no way of determining the profit; that is for the people who are running the service-works out between three and five per cent on the capital value of the four old steamers which the company are running, after taking the subsidy into account.
(Mr. Duff.]

This seems to be getting more complicated as we go along. The minister has shown us that the ships that had the contract last year from the government did not meet the requirements of the treaty, and yet they got the contract.
It was the former service that was continued. The West India islands are a consenting party to that arrangement. They pay something too.
Yes, I understand, but you let the contract to this company because you could not get anybody else that could meet the requirements of the treaty.
We had the Royal Mail Company carry on.

Under these circumstances
does not the minister think it would have been reasonable to have let the contract to the government's own ships?
They could not give the service.

They could not give the
service, yet the Royal Mail Company is complaining that the government ships are taking the trade.

My hon. friend has missed
the point. There are some islands that the Canadian ships cannot go into at all, and the complaint of the Royal Mail Line is that the Canadian boats go into the profitable islands and skip the others.
WThy should they not?

That is not keeping the
contract.

There is not
much profit in it for the tax payer of Canada.

The hon. member for Lunenburg has just said that he could prove to us that there was no ship belonging to the Canadian government that could be refitted to take part in this trade. I say that if he can prove that, now is the time to do it. It is no use proving it at some other time after this estimate has passed. If he has the proof, we ought to have it now.
Let us understand each other. Here is a contract with the West India islands. Does my hon. friend say that we should repudiate that contract and cancel the service?

I can answer the question of

I am sorry the minister was not able to provide the committee with information requested by [DOT]one of the members for Calgary, with regard to how much the West Indian government had paid this government as a part of its share of responsibility. It may amuse some of the members of committee to know that outside of that section, which has not been complied with very well up to date, there is another requirement. The agreement says:
If a subsidized steamship service is arranged for, the government of Canada will endeavour to secure the co-operation of the owners of such steamship service towards the provision of hotels and bungalows in the colonies, the governments of the colonies being prepared on their part to offer such facilities as may be practicable both as regards sites and financial assistance.
The main objection to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine and the Royal Mail Steam Packet appears to be the fact that you cannot equip the merchant marine with passenger accommodation, but, so far as I can see from the agreement, the only type of passenger who wants to go down there will be those who want a lazy holiday and not the business men. The business man will) any business instinct would never take the slow boat, not even the 12 knot boat if you had any. He would go to New York, make a rapid trip and get through with his business. The whole subsidy is to provide the wealthy people with opportunities for a lazy voyage. The agreement looks as though it were framed for that purpose. I have the greatest respect for the nautical knowledge of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), but I would submit that there are others in the House who know a little about it, not so much perhaps as he does. committee will allow me to be a little personal, I would say that sailing ships in which I am interested are doing business with the West Indies in competition with the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company and the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. These little ships, of which I am manager, go to Barbados and the other islands with Canadian products and bring back molasses and other commodities. For instance, this week I was home sending the schooner A. W. Chisholm to Trinidad with a cargo of cotton. These ships get no subsidy from this or any other government, they sail on their own bottoms, and if we lose money we grin and bear it. Consequently I agree with the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) that we should not pay subsidies if it is possible to avoid it. But a change has taken place since I made my speech in 1919 which makes it essential for us to pay this subsidy, if we are to continue the service to the West Indies. And the change is that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships are now engaging in the same trade and taking business which the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company should get. If a new contract is entered into by the Minister of Trade and Commerce with a reputable firm which will supply good ships, my opinion is that inside two or three years we will not have to pay any further subsidies because there will be sufficient business developed to enable such a line to be operated without assistance. But at present owing to the stupidity of some one, the Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships having been put in competition with the Royal Steam Packet Company's fleet, both lines are losing money, and as a result this parliament is compelled to vote a subsidy to maintain communication between the West Indies and the Maritime province ports. It would be suicidal to talk of discontinuing the subsidy now, for the shippers of the Maritime provinces would not be able to get their products to the West Indian markets, and consequently our farmers and fishermen would suffer. Therefore while I am opposed to subsidies in principle, I say it is necessary to have this subsidy voted, and I hope it will Ije agreed to.

The minister a moment ago in answer to a question from the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) stated that the contract was already let, and that therefore the money had to be voted. Am I right?	'

A contract was given for two years, but there is a clause in all these subsidy contracts that their continuance is subject to the vote of parliament. If parliament does not vote this money the contract ceases. But there is an obligation on the part of the Dominion to carry on this contract until March, 1924. And we are not the only parties to it; our fellow-Britishers in the West Indies are also concerned. We are trying to carry out our part of the contract. If my hon. friends desire to continue the argument all night, well and good. I have been in that game before, and I agree with the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Baxter) that nothing is to be gained by it. I never favoured -such tactics when I was opposition whip. If
my hon. friends say frankly they do not want to take the vote now, we can adjourn and go home lik.e decent men to-night, but we can stay here until August just as well as they can. But if hon. gentlemen are prepared after reasonable debate of the amendment to vote, I do not object to staying a little while longer.

May I submit to the committee that we are trying to act conscientiously and carefully? Some of us have gone into this matter with care, and we are trying to do our duty as we see it. There is no intention on anybody's part to hold up or unduly obstruct the business of the House, a,nd I think any such suggestions are rather unkind.
I am glad to have that assurance.
I understood the minister to say that we are obligated so far as this particular item is concerned to the amount of $340,000.

Whatever it is. Will the minister state shortly the actual terms of the contract existing between this company and the government under which this liability arises? I want to get particulars as to the nature of the service to be rendered and the tonnage of the boats to be used if any tonnage is provided for, or does the government simply say: You carry on the service fortnightly with these boats that you have got and we will pay you $340,000.

My hon. friend is right. That was the best arrangement we could make at that time. When the late government advertised for tenders for the improved service in order to carry out the contract, the tender that came in was not satisfactory. We considered that a basis of 7{ per cent on the invested capital was too uncertain, so we made an arrangement with the company to continue the service that had existed for many years and we paid them the same subsidy.

I am not going to make a speech, although I had a great deal of information that I wanted to give to the committee, but since I have been assured by my hon. friend from St. John and by hon. gentlemen opposite that they do not pay any attention to what is said anyway, it is unnecessary to make a speech. I understood the minister to say that he thought it advisable to subsidize an opposition line in order to secure competition which would result in lower freight rates for the Canadian people.

I hope my hon. friend did not understand me to say anything of the kind. I do not remember making any such statement.
I thought the minister did not remember having said that, buf. I am quite sure he said it.
Hansard will show.
Yes, I think it will show he made that statement.

There are two points I would like to mention before the vote is taken. A suggestion was made from the opposite side of the House that if the government took off the government boats and continued this service, in other words, gave a monopoly to the Royal Mail Line, in a very short time the profits presumably of the company would be such that there would be no further subsidy required. I would like to ask the committee if it has ever been on record in the history of Canada that any steamship company ceased to ask for a subsidy or to get it. Did the condition ever arise when a company would come forward and say that it did not require any further assistance? No, they have always asked for it, and they have always got it.
There is another phase of the question. The minister said that when he was calling for these contracts there was only one tenderer. Now if we do away with the opposition of the government boats and practically give a monopoly to this Royal Mail Packet Line, it will not be $340,000 that they will want in two years, but five or six hundred thousand dollars because they will take deliberate, cold-blooded advantage of the fact that they have no competitor in the field. You cannot dig up a competing line in a week or two. The company that has a monopoly stampedes you. I have had some experience out west with that kind of thing. When the contract has nearly expired the people served by this line are naturally very anxious to see it maintained, and the company that has been given a monopoly knows that they have driven off competitors, and they get busy and hold up the government. We may lose money by the continuation of the merchant marine service down there, but we shall save it in the other way by stopping a monopoly, and if there was no opposition that would be the inevitable result.
I have only this to say as regards the vote: There is no question that as the government have entered into the contract parliament will have to vote the money, and judging from the numbers here the government will carry the 
vote. I hope they will, because I realize they have to carry out this contract. But I think there is a great deal of light to be let into this system of subsidies all over Canada, and I do not think the discussion to-night has been time ill-spent. I intend to support the amendment of the hon. member for Bow River, not that I am in favour of doing away with the vote, but as an expression of sympathy with him and those who support him in the suggestion made from across the floor that they are animated by improper motives, as if they had no right to do so if they chose.

I do not
want the committee to be under the impression that we in this corner of the House are moving this amendment from pique or anything of that kind, nor because we fail to recognize the sacredness of a contract. I submit that it is a protest from the people of Canada whom we are here to represent against the government of Canada entering into contracts that compel the subsequent voting of money by the members of the House.
Amendment negatived.

Item agreed to.
